speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks, I should like to pay one compliment to my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King); I should like to compliment him upon the physical feat which he performed yesterday in talking for four hours to this house. I will not discuss the mental aspect of it, except as I go along, but I gladly offer him a compliment on the physical feat he performed. And since I have only forty minutes at my disposal I am sure he will forgive me if I pay him no other compliment during my remarks.
We all greatly enjoyed the speech of the right hon. gentleman, particularly the last part of it, the last half hour or so, when, during that peroration he worked himself up into a frenzy of righteous indignation because of alleged neglect of the unemployed by the present government. It reminded those of us who are old-timers in the house, those who have been here for quite a number of years, of the days in 1920 when the right hon. gentleman was making the same kind of speeches. Yesterday he even discussed orders in council and the cost of living, and I thought, by an accident perhaps, Senate reform might drop from his lips; I have no doubt that long before the next election he will be a Senate reformer once again as he was before the days of 1920. In other words, Mr. Speaker, he adopted the role of the demagogue which he assumed in the old days of opposition, when he was a defender of the downtrodden and the oppressed of all classes. In opposition my right hon. friend is the most politically virtuous politician in this country. He fairly tore the purple out of the skies when he was condemning the terrible sins of this government, and comparing the multi-millionaires and millionaires of this government with the labouring people.
My right hon. friend has an unfortunate memory; he forgets the early years of his own association with millionaires, when he
was pleasantly-and I may say without offence, profitably-associated with one of the greatest exploiting millionaires this continent has ever produced, a man whose unsavoury reputation in his dealings with labour still sticks to the association which my right hon. friend had with him, and which I fear will stick for a long time.
I was rather glad to see my right hon. friend take the attitude of not accepting the subamendment of the party in the far comer, because during the debate on the address he did accept the subamendment brought forward by that party in a rather humiliating manner, I thought, from the standpoint of his party. He swallowed it; he swallowed his own amendment, hook, line and sinker, but the story goes that some of his own party walked out on him and refused to follow his lead in that vote, so at this time he could not do the same thing.
Then my right hon. friend spent a good deal , of time in dealing with advertising. He seems to forget that the late Jim Robb, who was Minister of Trade and Commerce for some years, and Jim Malcolm, who was also Minister of Trade and Commerce for some years, used to put out the same kind of advertising in the press of this country in the name of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I heard many protests raised against that practice on the floor of this house. My right lion, friend particularly worked himself up because of that phrase "Canada first." That still sticks in his crop, if I may use that expression. I suppose he prefers the old cry of "Washington first" rather than "Canada first." Well, I will admit quite frankly that probably this government have made some mistakes; no doubt they will commit others, but at the same time they remain a Canada first government and are proud of it.
Referring also to advertising, I felt that the right hon. gentleman was perhaps unfortunate in his references, because recently there has been an airing in the courts of some advertising which his own government took on in London. Apparently his government, according to the press, were not only satisfied to pay the advertising bills, but also a nice fat fee of $5,000 which was to go to one of their political supporters.
Then, Mr. Speaker, he dealt with taxes, and he put up that old argument that taxes were lowered by the late government. How you can lower taxes and at the same time take more taxes from the people always has been a puzzle to this side of the house. I make the statement without fear of contradiction, Mr. Speaker, that the government

The Budget-Mr. Manion
of the right hon. gentleman took more money in taxes from the people of this country, during his years of premiership, than any other government ever took in a similar number of years in Canadian history.
The right hon. gentleman also spoke of the Welland canal, and he made a statement which he should have hesitated to make, because he has made it several times previously and I have tried to correct him. I will say again that the hon. gentleman was mistaken. We did not extend the contracts more than they are extended in the ordinary course of events. We carried on with the same contractors to whom my right hon. friend's government gave the contracts; we carried on at the same prices. These contractors, according to the Department of Justice, had a right to go on with their work, whether we liked it or not, and we had to pay the bill. That is the truth of the Welland canal matter, so I hope we will not hear statements of that kind again.
Then my right hon. friend worked himself up into that astonishing peroration on unemployment. He spoke of prosperity again. Well, Mr. Speaker, I was not far behind him out on his trip through the prairie provinces and British Columbia, and he started out with that talk of prosperity during the campaign. Some of his friends, however, told me they were afraid he would be mobbed before he finished, because there were so many unemployed at that time. The unemployment situation in Canada then was just as severe as it is now, if not more so.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I say it was at least as severe as and probably more severe than is the case at the present time, but then the right hon. gentleman and his ministers were talking about prosperity in this country. Why, the right hon. gentleman stood on the floor of this house and made the statement that there was no unemployment in this country. He made the further statement that he would not give a five cent piece for the relief of unemployment to any province of this country under a Conservative regime, and at that time there were six provinces with Conservative governments. Then he turned, as though he had discovered the villain in the piece, and said, "the Prime Minister laughs." No wonder the Prime Minister laughed; who would not laugh at such an attitude as that taken by the right hon. gentleman? Not only did the Prime Minister laugh; we all laughed when we thought of the attitude of the right hon. gentleman in connection with

unemployment when he had the power to help conditions, as contrasted with the attitude he takes now when he has no power to help.
Then my right hon. friend went on to deal with the railway situation in Canada, and I wish to spend most of my time on that subject because I am somewhat familiar with it. I believe the last person in this country to take a critical attitude towards a Conservative government in regard to railways is the leader of the Liberal party, because from 1900 to 1904, and perhaps again in 1911, there was an opportunity to put this country for all time in an easy position as far as railways were concerned. Yet my right hon friend's predecessor, as leader of the Liberal party at that time, not only permitted one transcontinental railway to be built, but permitted and almost insisted, or at least arranged, that two transcontinental railways should be built, in addition to the Canadian Pacific railway. He it was who went into the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme, with the old Grand Trunk, and arranged to construct the National Transcontinental in association with it, and it was he who, before going out of power in 1911, guaranteed to Mackenzie and Mann another $35,000,000 to extend their line from the great lakes east to Atlantic tidewater. Thus three transcontinental railways, were projected and built, and because of those two extra railways we have had the terribly oppressive condition in regard to railways that this country has been experiencing: We overbuilt in railways, as everyone knows. Had the right hon. leader of the Liberal party of that day had the vision to insist that the Grand Trunk in the east be linked up with the Canadian Northern in the west, we would have had but two transcontinental systems and we would have had no railway problem in this country at all. It was the duplication involved in the second and third transcontinental lines that put this country in- its present position. To-day we find that Great Britain, for example, has eight times as many people per mile of railway as we have in Canada; Germany has seven times as many; France five times as many and the United States over twice as many, and that condition is entirely due to the Liberal government of a quarter of a century ago. The result was that in 1918 and 1919-and of course the war complicated matters-'both these railway projects were left on the doorstep of the government. I will proceed to show that it is largely due to the late government that the difficulties of the national railways are very severe.
To-day, sir, we have the unpopular role of questioning the accounts and expenditures of

The Budget-Mr. Manion
the Canadian National Railways and telling the public the facts in that connection. I shall endeavour to show why that questioning is necessary. Between 1926 and 1928 there were boom conditions throughout the world; there were bounding revenues on the Canadian National. In 1928 the Canadian National Railways had a net operating revenue above all expenditures of $54,000,000, which was more than the interest owing to the public during that year; but in the following year, 1929, the net operating revenue had dropped by $13,000,000 to $41,000,000, which was $9,000,000 below the interest owing to the public during that year. Yet in 1929, the second last year of the late government and a preelection year, that government permitted and I expect encouraged commitments amounting to $270,000,000, and I am going to give the details, which are as follows:
Temporary financing carry-over
from 1928	$ 40,000,000
Ordinary budget requirements	53,000,000

eastern lines deficit	 9,000,000
Statutory authorizations outstanding	  22,000,000
1929-three-year branch line
program	 30,000,000
Montreal terminal scheme.. .	50,000,000
Acquisition of railways. .	. .	30,000,000
Equipment issues	 18,000,000
Refunding requirements.. ..	18,000,000
Total	$270,000,000
In that year, 1929, there was added to the funded debt of the national railways $145,000,000. In addition there was carried over into 1930 unfunded debt amounting to $32,000,000. If you consider that an amount of $145,000,000 means an annual interest charge against the national railways of $7,000,000, you realize the responsibility which the then government assumed. That amount of $145,000,000 was within ten million dollars of the amount of the total increase of funded debt in the six previous years.
On August 1, 1930, when we came into power, there were commitments amounting to $158,000,000 over which we had no control, and some of which still exist. Yet in 1930, that very year, the gross operating revenue of the Canadian National Railways was down by $3,000,000 as compared with 1923, and the interest to the public was up by $18,000,000 or $19,000,000 also as compared with 1923. Moreover, in 1927 they had made a three year branch line program and it was unfinished, but in 1929, the preelection year, they brought in a 1929-32 program which amounted to S30,000,000 on top of the other unfinished program of the previous three years.
It might be asked: What part of that program was unnecessary? What was done that the then government urged the national railways to do? I am quite certain that I am within my rights in stating that much of the expenditure was pushed on by the government of that day. There were such things as the $2,000,000 Halifax hotel which was just about as much needed as a fifth wheel on a coach; a $4,000,000 hotel in Saskatoon where I am informed by the best authorities that a million dollar hotel would have difficulty in paying; a $9,000,000 hotel in Vancouver. The much maligned "shadow" government of 1926 passed an order in council for the building of the hotel at Vancouver, but it was for a $3,500,000 hotel to satisfy that city in regard to arrangements made by Mackenzie and Mann. That, however, was increased in 1929 to $9,000,000. Then there were the steamers on the Pacific coast. They even had in their estimate a hotel at Prince Rupert amounting to $600,000. These were all brought in by the Canadian National in association with the government of that day in a preelection year.
May I say that if we had a few more years with expenditures like those of 1929, there would be no Canadian National Railways to tell a tale. I am not blaming Sir Henry Thornton and his officials. They were enthusiastic, perhaps over-enthusiastic, as all engineering officials are, in dealing with a big organization. They like to build an organization of that kind into a magnificent institution, and that was the object of Sir Henry Thornton. But the government of that day was the trustee not only of the people of Canada but of the Canadian National Railways, and after a year's survey I can find no evidence that at any time the late government showed any signs of realizing its responsibility as a trustee of the people of Canada and the Canadian National Railways. I wish to add that Sir Henry Thornton and his officials deserve a great deal of credit for the excellent work done by them in consolidating diverse and competing railways, in bringing about a fine esprit de corps amongst the officers and men and in bending their best efforts to build up a great transportation system to compete with the Canadian Pacific. But I do not give any credit to the late government for the fact that they pressed forward scores of millions of dollars of expenditure by the Canadian National Railways that the railways would have been better without.
In regard to the Canadian National Railways so many figures have been put on
The Budget-Mr. Manion

Hansard by various speakers that I am going to give a brief resume of the position, as was done by my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) in a straightforward discussion when he presented the budget. I shall show in brief the position and the responsibility that we have in that regard. There are only two items that are important in the balance sheet:
Funded debt unmatured.. $1,168,000,000 Dominion of Canada account 1,330,000,000
Total	$2,498,000,000
Or, in round figures, $2,500,000,000. The amount of $1,168,000,000 is money owing to the public lenders of funds; that is the bonds and debenture stocks that were issued. These consist of securities guaranteed by the government to the extent of some $926,000,000 and unguaranteed securities to the extent of $242,000,000. The interest on the debt to the public amounted in 1930 to $53,000,000, or more than $1,000,000 a week. It was that interest to the public that the Canadian National Railways were short of paying last year by $29,000,000, but they were also short the $32,000,000 of interest owing on government loans. In fact, that has never been and probably never will be paid. The whole national income of Canada in 1900 was only $50,000,000, and when you consider that the interest owing to the public alone by the national railways is now more than $50,000,000, a year you realize the magnitude of that figure.
Let me give a few other figures in explanation of the item of $1,330,000,000.-Dominion of Canada account. This comprises loans amounting to $60-1,000,000, two-thirds of which was spent upon capital and the balance on deficits. But the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), speaking the other day, suggested that that $604,000,000 should be wiped out altogether. I do not know why two-thirds of that amount should be wiped out seeing that it has gone into the property.
Then there is interest amounting to $322,000,000 that has accrued on that amount of $604,000,000 during the years, but unfortunately, not one cent of it has been paid, and I do not think we can hope for repayment in the future. The third item is the appropriations amounting to $403,000,000 covering the cost of the Intercolonial, the Prince Edward Island Railway and the National Transcontinental. Those three items amount to $1,330,000,000, which is the actual cost in money or in loss to the public of the Canadian National Railways. There are some who say that that interest on that $604,000,000 should be wiped
[Mr. Manion.l
out, but is it not a fact that if that money had not been spent on the Canadian National, before and since amalgamation, that money would have been available to lessen the debt of the country? Therefore it has been a straight loss.
But that is not all of the responsibility of Canada. In addition to the $1,330,000,000 made up of loans, $604,000,000, interest, $332,000,000 and appropriations of $403,000,000, there are guarantees amounting to $926,000,000. If you add those together, you get a Canadian government responsibility of $2,256,000,000, and according to the public accounts, the whole war and demobilization cost was $1,695,000,000, or about $500,000,000 or $600,000,000 less than the cost of the national railways to Canada so far including the guarantees. Those are stupendous amounts. I think the Toronto Telegram was right in saying that is Canada's second national debt. What makes it the more serious is the fact that during the present year, 1931, the income of the Canadian National Railway is decreasing. There was published in the press only this morning the decrease for the last week for which the accounting is completed, and compared with the corresponding week last year the decrease in income is over one million dollars. In other w'ords, the revenues of the railways are going down, and the deficit on interest to the public, instead of being $29,000,000 this year, must, unless something miraculous happens, be more than that amount.
Therefore I have laid before the house the official figures because I want this house and the country to realize the great responsibility of the country towards the Canadian National Railway, and the great investment which the country has in that railway. I submit that in view of the magnitude of that investment it is our duty as a government to examine the figures of expenditure and revenue of the Canadian National Railway. It is our duty not only as a government but as loyal Canadians, and as friends of the Canadian National Railway itself, to do that. Our desire is that not only the Canadian National Railway but the Canadian Pacific Railway as well shall be successful. We want them to work together in healthy competition and reasonable cooperation, giving economic management and fair rates to the people of this country. I submit again that the clear-cut statement of facts given by my right hon. leader in his budget statement was a straightforward and necessary statement which the people must have in order to realize the position of the Canadian National Railway as it affects the people of this country, and I say that the statement that is being foolishly

The Budget-Mr. Manion
made by some of the press of my right hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, that we are enemies of the Canadian National Railway, is simply an untruth. Any man who is an enemy of the Canadian National Railways is not a good Canadian, and therefore as I consider this a good Canadian government, and that we are at least good Canadians, we are not the enemies of the Canadian National Railway, but its friends, desirous of looking after its best interests.
The principle of public ownership is not at stake, because we are into public ownership to the extent I have shown by over $2,000,000,000, and we are being asked this very year to guarantee securities of the railway to the amount of over $104,000,000, for public ownership. I say without fear of contradiction by people who think properly that when the national railways have attained to the position where they neither require guarantees nor cash assistance from the people of Canada in vast amounts, then and not till then should their accounts be free from examination by the members of this house. I say further that I have talked this matter over several times with Sir Henry Thornton, and he agrees with every word that I have said so far as the necessity for an examination of the accounts and the need for economy goes. Only yesterday in the railways and shipping committee Sir Henry Thornton explained during a period of one hour and a half the efforts they are making to bring about economies that are absolutely necessary at the present time, and I invite my hon. friend from North Waterloo, who is not in his seat at the moment, but who connected my right hon. leader with another speaker on this side of the house who is not in the government, and who he said made an attack on the Canadian National Railway, to ask Sir Henry Thornton at the meeting of that committee tomorrow-and I will invite Sir Henry Thornton to answer frankly-if he is not perfectly satisfied with the attitude of this government towards the Canadian National Railway in every possible way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I do not think Sir
Henry Thornton has ever been afraid to express himself frankly. He gets very good support throughout the country and I do not think he would hesitate to -express himself quite frankly. If he did, it is certainly not my fault. Proof that the management themselves realize the need for economy is found in the fact that they have within the last
few days organized a finance committee, made up of the president, the deputy minister, Mr. Smart, who represents the government in my absence, and Mr. Gerard Ruel, one of the vice-presidents, the duty of which committee will be to investigate every expenditure of the railway. Further proof is found in the fact that the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, at the request of my right hon. leader, have for some months been endeavouring to cut out unnecessary duplications and unnecessary competition, and they have done so to the extent that they have made a saving, they claim, of something like one million dollars a year each by cutting out unnecessary duplication and unnecessary services.
I admit that our lot is not a very pleasant one in regard to checking up the expenditures, but it is a very necessary one. I submit that the motto of the Canadian National Railway should be: Care, caution and proper economy. When you realize that from 1923 to 1930 the cash and guarantees to the Canadian National Railway amounted to something over $490,000,000, and when you realize that the actual net debt of Canada on March 31, 1914, amounted to $336,000,000, or, in other words, the cash and guarantees to the railway have been 50 per cent greater than our whole national debt before the war, you will realize why these investigations are advisable.
It might be asked, how a government can interfere with a railway in any way without interfering with maintenance and efficiency? I say that it can interfere as the government of my right hon. friend had the opportunity to interfere in regard to some of the capital expenditures I have mentioned earlier in my remarks. I read recently in one of the outstanding papers of Canada, the statement that these expensive hotels were necessary because they added indirectly to the passenger train revenues. I wondered if that was correct, and so I had an investigation made by the officers, and the report of the officers to me was that the passenger revenue loss in 1926 was $4,000,000, and the passenger loss in 1930 was $20,000,000. These great expenditures on passenger service, therefore, are not giving the return they should give.
There is another question on which I wish to touch in regard to the Canadian National, and that is the question of refinancing. I see many statements by editorial writers, and receive many letters, to the effect that there should be a refinancing of the Canadian National. I read in one of the Toronto papers only last evening that if a proper refinancing
The Budget-Mr. Manion

was made of the Canadian National Railway, the road would be able to pay its way. Now the only way you could put the road in a position to pay its own way would be to wipe off the $1,330,000,000 which it owes to the government and a part of the $1,168,000,000 which it owes to the public. The only scheme of refinancing which was put up by the Canadian National itself was put up to Mr. Dunning when he was Minister of Railways in 1928. The scheme then was to write off some $800,000,000 of the capital structure, which was made up of capital stocks adjudged valueless, deficits, and interest, amounting to a little over $800,000,000. Adding those stocks to which I have not paid any attention in the figures which I have given, but which form a considerable part of the capital liabilities to the $1,330,000,000, you have government account of $1,600,000,000. If you wipe out $800,000,000 from $1,600,000,000, you still have left $800,000,000 on which interest would accrue, and as not a cent of interest has ever been paid to the government I say that the refinancing could not possibly be of any use at this time, because the $29,000,000 that was short last year was not on government account, but on the $1,168,000,000 owing to the investing public. Therefore, any refinancing scheme that has thus far been proposed could not possibly put the Canadian National Railway in a position to carry itself. I have discussed this question many times with Sir Henry Thornton, and I have in my desk a letter from him stating that he does not consider that at the present time it would be of any use to propose any refinancing scheme to the government and to parliament.
There is one other matter that I wish to mention, and that is the public demands not only upon the Canadian National but upon the Canadian Pacific as well. We get demands from all over Canada for rate reductions and capital investments. I have requests before me to-day for capital investments in stations, hotels, branch lines, bridges, and so forth, for the Canadian National Railway, amounting to $200,000,000. The people of Canada cannot have it both ways. They cannot have rate reductions on all possible occasions, and capital expansion in every direction, and at the same time have the Canadian National Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway remain in a sound economic position. In addition to the demands for rate reductions, the railways during the last few years have had to meet severe motor bus and motor truck competition, which has been without regulation. It is not fair, I say here to-day, to either of these two great transcontinental

systems, with their expensive roadbed, their high priced equipment and heavy taxes, that they should have to meet the competition of motor bus and motor truck lines running on public highways that have been built partly out of the tax-es on the railways themselves. These bus and truck lines come under no regulation, and I believe that in this country as in other parts of the world we shall be compelled to put into effect some method of control.
I might be asked, what is the outlook for the Canadian National Railway. After a fairly thorough study of the question I would say this:	My feeling is that there is no occasion for panic if wise and prudent direction and control are exercised. Provided that certain conditions obtain which I shall hereinafter mention, I think that within five years we will have a much more cheerful story to tell for the Canadian National Railways than we have to-day. The world is going forward, and I consider the present depression will pass as other depressions have passed, although my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition last night looked at the depression through very blue goggles. Since he has become leader of the opposition he is very much more pessimistic than when he was in power. Of course I will agree that that is an effect of being in opposition. I have no doubt my right hon. friend opposite feels there is a gentleman who can handle the affairs of this country very much more satisfactorily than can my right hon. leader, although probably the right hon. gentleman opposite is much too modest to mention the name of that gentleman.
The following are the conditions:	If the
depression passes, if unwise capital expenditures are not indulged in, if costly advertising stunts are eliminated, if proper economic management is brought into play and if the people of this country are reasonable in their demands as to freight rates and capital expenditures, I think within five years from now there will be a very much more hopeful and cheerful picture in connection with both the great railways of Canada than there is at the present time.
May I say in closing that the real friends of the national railways are those who believe in care, caution and economy in the policies of the road. The real enemies of the road are those who, consciously or unconsciously, advocate extravagant or unnecessary expenditures in connection with the operation of the road. The course of this government and of hon. members on this side of the house, is the only loyal course the people of

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)
Canada can adopt, so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, not only towards the road but towards the people of Canada themselves.
Sir, I have spoken much more hurriedly than I otherwise would have done because I had a great deal of ground to cover. I have however placed a great many facts before the house, and I submit again that my right hon. friend should be the last man to say that the present government is not acting fairly towards the railway company. I would ask my right hon. friend opposite to remember that it was his government that permitted, if it did not actually encourage, those immense capital expenditures the interest upon which is to-day a very heavy load upon the national railways.

May I, quietly and humbly, present to this house a quotation from Hansard of May 13, 1930:
There is in medicine an unscientific type of practitioner who when he does not know how to diagnose a case takes ten or a dozen drugs, jumbles them together in a prescription and offers it to the patient, hoping that if one therapeutic bullet does not hit the disease, another may. That is what is sarcastically called a "gun-shot" prescription. This budget is a "gun-shot" budget, the government hoping that if one political bullet does not bring down what I may call the prey, another bullet may do so.
The author of that wonderful paragraph was the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion). And to show the delightful consistency of the minister may I quote from his address as delivered in the city of Vancouver during the last election campaign. He said this:
One of the policies of our party is that we don't want any more immigrants till we can look after our own people.
Hear, hear! Now, let us read what the hon. member said in this parliament, as it is reported in Hansard of May 22, 1929, at page 2746, when the hon. member supported that dramatic and exorbitant scheme of his confrere, General McRae, the chief opposition whip:
We have one of the greatest countries in the world and if it were properly handled it should be the mecca for all the desirable peoples in all the overcrowded portions of the earth.
Yes, China, Japan and even Russia! My hon. friend was then inviting them all. Further he stated:
My complaint is not so much that the number of British immigrants is not larger, as that our immigration of all classes is much too small. The question is often asked how many can we absorb in this country?
And once again:
I submit that we can take many more immigrants of all kinds.
And again:
I submit that we have a need for people of all classes.

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)
And again:
If our country is as prosperous as the right hon. the Prime Minister and some of his followers claim it is, we should he able to absorb hundreds of thousands of all classes of immigrants from all countries.
Exhibit 3, Mr. Speaker-Manion on the sales tax. To-day my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways and Canals, is favourable to an increase in sales tax from one to 4 per cent. What did he say on May 8, 1929, while on this side of the house, and speaking for the official opposition:
We think the sales tax should be wiped out altogether.
Exhibit 4, Mr. Speaker-Manion on trade, during the regime of the wicked Liberal administration. We find on March 8, 1929, at page 791 of Hansard, the following statements of the present Minister of Railways and Canals in his address on the budget:
For example, the Argentine buys from us nearly twice as much as we buy from them; Belgium two and a half times as much; Brazil over three times as much; Chile nearly seven times as much; China over six times as much; Denmark twenty-five times as much; Germany two and a half times as much; Japan three and a half times as much; the Netherlands over five times as much; Portugal eight times as much. But the United States buys from us only one-half of the amount she sells to us.
What a wonderful tribute by the hon. Minister of Railways to the trade policies of the Liberal party in 1929! Now let me give the last of these exhibits in regard to the delightful consistency of my hon. and consistent friend. Speaking in this house on April 2, 1930, he is reported in Hansard at page 1201 as follows:
I submit to the Prime Minister that the people of this country are anxious for frank and candid statements from the government at the present time on all matters of public policy.
The hon. gentleman was speaking in regard to unemployment. All this session we have been pressing the Prime Minister and his colleagues for a declaration of policy on behalf of unemployment, and all the satisfaction we have got so far is the long distance interview with the absentee Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson) in my province of British Columbia.
But the inconsistency of my hon. friend belongs not only to the past; it belongs to the immediate present. He began his tremendous indictment of the late Liberal administration this afternoon with respect to the Canadian National Railways by saying that in 1904 the then Liberal government was responsible for certain things. I believe that my hon. friend

was of age in 1904, I believe that he was then a strong supporter of the Liberal administration.

I shall
never forget the reception accorded the Dunning budget by the press of London; Conservative, Liberal and Labour papers were a solid chorus in their commendation. The diehard Conservative Morning Post stated:
The Dominion of Canada has taken another step along the line of their traditional policy of giving preference to imperial trade, and since changes in tariff cannot fail to benefit the mother country, our first impulse is to express the gratitude which we are certain the British public feels.
The Daily Express, Conservative, said:
The Dunning budget constitutes the greatest advance in imperial relations we have seen since the war.
The London Times, Conservative, said:
The advantages offered by Canada to British industry are offered without any bargaining or corresponding concessions and the spirit which prompted them will be appreciated as much as their actual economic effect in helping British trade at a time when help is badly needed.
Mr. J. L. Garvin, in the London Observer, expressed this opinion:
The Canadian budget is one of those rare strokes of policy which illuminate the realities of empire.
The Times Trade Supplement contained the following:
There can be no doubt that Mr. Dunning's budget in the Canadian parliament is the most important preparatory step that has been taken by any government since the Imperial conference of 1926 towards the ideal of closer imperial economic cooperation.
The Congress of Federal Chambers of Commerce passed this resolution:
The council of the empire reiterates its belief that the wide extension of imperial preference is the most effective means of bringing about a greater measure of imperial economic cohesion.
The Hon. Neville Chamberlain, at Birmingham, said:
We shall have a chance of showing what we can do to supply goods Canada cannot supply herself.

the president of the National Dairy Council say in this regard? Listen to the man whose views as quoted last evening were acclaimed 'by my hon. friends opposite. Speaking at the twelfth annual meeting of the National Dairy Council, held at the Royal Alexandra hotel, Winnipeg, on March 18 and If) of this year, he said:
At the last meeting, an appeal to the tariff board was decided upon. The hearings were held in January, 1930, and several months later the government announced an increase in the butter tariff of precisely the amount we asked for. At this point I wish to remind you very definitely that we took the view that a tariff of four cents per pound against the southern dominions, where the imported butter all came from, was about as high a tariff as the industry could obtain any permanent benefit from. We used the argument that a tariff higher than four cents would damage the cheese industry and would introduce very wide and unmanageable fluctuations of price into the butter market if we were to alternate from an import to an export basis and back again, as we have done many times in the past forty years. Our conclusion was that the amount of the present protection would prove to be excessive in the long run and would have to be modified, so that the untoward events of the future cannot be laid at the door of this council. With respect to New Zealand, as already intimated to parliament, the government of Canada has proposed to the government of that dominion that a direct trade agreement be negotiated to supersede the present arrangement.	_
We hope to be able to arrange for meetings of representatives of both countries in the near future in order to endeavour to reach a mutually satisfactory agreement. In any eyent, the present arrangement will cease on October twelfth next. Following that date, Canada will extend her full British preference to New Zealand, pending the completion of a direct agreement.
My province is particularly hurt by the abandonment of the preference. From 1922 to 1930, imports from New Zealand increased from $2,000,000 to $16,000,000, while exports increased from $4,000,000 to $19,000,000. In

our trade wdth Austi'alia our imports in 1929 amounted to $3,500,000 and our exports to $19,500,000.
I remember hearing the Minister of Trade and Commerce condemning the Australian treaty because apparently the balance of trade was too favourable to Canada, and at the same time condemning the French treaty because the balance of trade was unfavourable to this country. By the way, I trust that the government will take steps immediately to negotiate with France with a view to removing the increase in their tariff against British Columbia salmon going into that country.
Let me now refer briefly to the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) as reported at page 2309 of Hansard. The minister said:
Now I want to refer to farm exports just for a moment. Farm exports have fallen off. But let me give my hon. friend opposite a very unpleasant reminder. During the years that they held office-and mark you, we are now discussing that portion of my hon. friend's remarks in which he dealt with the fiscal policy of this country injuring exports; I want that to be borne in mind-during their term of office from 1921 to 1930, farm exports to the United States dropped from $162,880,000 to $40,841,000, or a falling off in nine years of no less than 75 per cent.
That statement is entirely misleading. Those are not the figures for nine years. They were taken from page 794 of the Commercial Intelligence Journal and they deal only with the ten-month period ended April 31, 1930, and that is a decrease of 75 per cent spread over a period of nine years. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce had pursued the figures down to April, 1931, he would have found that there was a reduction from $40,000,000 to $20,000,000, or 50 per cent in one year as against 75 per cent in nine years. My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) dealt ably with this matter the other day, as did my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Reid). Let me give some figures with reference to coal production. According to the records Nova Scotia's production is 6,250,000 tons; New Brunswick's, 209,000 tons; or a total for the maritime provinces of 6,459,000. The coal output of Saskatchewan is 578,000 tons; that of Alberta, 5,704,000, and that of the Crowsnest 738,000, or a total of 7,020,000 tons. Vancouver island's output amounts to 1,107,000 tons.
After making the estimate as generous as possible, the only benefit Vancouver island

will derive is the paltry sum of $20,000, whereas we estimate that, on a total output of 1,000,000 tons, we are entitled proportionately to $163,000.

If Premier Bennett had gone into office with the one object of ruining the coal industry of Vancouver island, he could not have taken any surer means than are included in his budget proposals. . . . He has not even made an attempt to formulate a national fuel policy. Let me give another brief quotation from this journal:
Bennett was elected in Canada as the high priest of the gospel of protection. He went to London shortly after being elected, and came back to Canada, publicly accused by the British Minister of Labour as a master of humbug. I do not care to come back to something my hon. friend would not understand. The amendment to the amendment, moved by my hon. friends to my left, deals with the question of currency. I hope I shall not be out of order in this respect if I'disagree with my right hon. leader. In my opinion-and it is only my personal opinion-the question of currency is at the present time far more vital to the solution of our economic problems than any dispute about the tariff situation in Canada. I disagree entirely with the nature of the subamendment in dealing with the currency situation. I do not believe that depreciation of currency is the solution of this question. If my hon. friends had been somewhat more temperate in their amendment, if they had advocated the abandonment of gold as the single monetary standard of the world, without going so far as to propose an unlimited increase of paper currency, which is practically the consequence of their subamendment, I should have felt like giving them a measure of support.
I do believe, Mr. Speaker, that to-day there are some very distinguished economists in the world-I do not pretend to be one-who are emphasizing the doctrine that because of the disparity between the price of gold and the price of commodities, instead of a monometallic system there should be a duo-metallic system, or at least a standardization of the relative currency values of one or the other metal. If my hon. friends had only gone as far as that I should have been glad to support their amendment. In passing I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister upon the conference he had with Mr. J. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I desire
to refer to the very important problem of unemployment, Mr. Speaker, and I shall conclude in probably five minutes. In amplification of the concluding portion of the remarks of my right bon. leader last evening in regard to a conference on unemployment, I wish to remind this house that item 426 of the supplementary estimates of the session of 1930 read as follows:
(Mr. I. Mackenzie.]
To provide for a conference of representatives of dominion and provincial governments, municipalities, transportation companies and industrial and labour organizations to consider methods of cooperation in furthering continuous employment throughout Canada during the winter months.
So the declaration of policy made by my right hon. leader yesterday afternoon is only an amplification of his pronouncement of policy made in this house last year, for which money was voted.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to stress, as other members have done, the tremendous national character of the unemployment situation. I have had telegrams from the city of Vancouver pointing out that the situation there is exceedingly serious, and I desire to inform hon. gentlemen opposite that if ever in the history of Canada cooperation and national leadership were required, they are required at the present time. As far as I am personally concerned, if the administration announces to this house a policy in regard to unemployment which will look after the starving people and provide for them food, clothing and shelter during the winter of 1931, I shall be prepared to cooperate during the rest of this session as much as possible in regard to legislation before the house.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I submit that it is the distinct duty of the government to proclaim to this parliament gathered together, as soon as they possibly can, what is to be their policy in regard to next winter. I wish to speak not at all in a partisan way in regard to this tremendous national crisis when I warn the administration seriously and solemnly that there are ominous murmurings to-day throughout Canada. Unless adequate preparation is made in good time by this administration it will be not only this government which will be endangered; it will be the system of government we have in Canada to-day. Sir, my contribution to this study of the unemployment situation would be along the lines of that famous utterance of that great Canadian patriot, Wiliam Lyon Mackenzie :
Well may I love the poor; greatly may I esteem the humble and the lowly, for poverty and adversity were my nurses, and in youth were want and misery my familiar friends.
I should like now to recommend to this house consideration of the concluding words of a great book written by the grandson of William Lyon Mackenzie:
Is it too much to believe that having witnessed humanity pass through its Geth-semane, having seen its agony in its garden of fears, having beheld its crucifixion upon the ci'oss of militarism, labour and capital will yet

The Budget-Mr. Geary
bring to a disconsolate and broken-hearted *world the one hope that is theirs alone to bring, and that in the acceptance of the principles which hold deliverance from the scourges that beset mankind they will roll back the stone from the door of the world's sepulchre to-day and give to humanity the promise of its resurrection to a more abundant life.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the government once more that if they will bring down measures to protect our unemployed, perhaps by way of a great national loan in order to look after the problems of unemployment during the next year and a half and to protect men who are being forced out of business by foreclosure proceedings instituted by our financial institutions; if the government are prepared to issue a great national loan and bring down their policy on the floor of this house, I for one am prepared to remain silent with regard to any other discussions which may arise, and to support them in providing for our comrades throughout the length and breadth of this great dominion of ours.

Mr. Speaker, that the remarks of my hon. and gallant friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) were not displeasing to this side of the house is, I think, made sufficiently plain by the fact that we protested against his speech being cut off. I shall not follow my hon. friend through the course of his remarks, but in the vehemence of an early excitement he indulged in attacks upon my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion). These attacks will be met easily, if they are worth meeting, by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, and I shall not attempt to take his part. Suffice it to say that the hon. member rather upbraided the minister for the early part of his speech, in which he accused the minister of descending to personalities, but my hon. friend did not hesitate to do that very thing.
The speech of the right hon. Prime Minister was long; it bespoke an endurance upon which I congratulate him, and more than that, it established a record for the right hon. gentleman of remaining longest in the air.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I refer to my right hon.
friend the leader of the opposition; I mentioned that the person to whom I referred had been longest in the air. The delight one might have in listening to the right hon. gentleman was somewhat marred for those of us who have been in the house during previous sessions by the fact that we have had
it all before. The right hon. gentleman loves to tell the old, old story, and the tales of the prosperity that attended his regime are very familiar to all of us. He ascribes to himself and to Providence, in the order named, the prosperity that he claims to have existed during the last eight years, but when we come to that bad period of his last year in office, he withdraws himself from the partnership and leaves poor Providence to bear all the onus of the disturbance. He is not quite fair; indeed, he has never been quite fair in his reference to the condition of affairs that existed at the time he came into power. He has always refused to admit that the grants to railways during the preceding years had any bearing whatever upon the financial condition as it existed. What my right hon. friend well knows, as Mr. Fielding said in 1922, is that during the period of the war the country had been very heavily taxed. Money was being given on all hands; people were cheerfully paying taxes and making contributions in the country's cause, and it was not within the power of any government which might have then been in power to exact more in taxes from the people than did the government of the war period. So necessarily, and I think largely with the consent of the house, advances were made to the different railways, amounting in the end to some $500,000,000. That went into the capital debt, but my right hon. friend has always insisted that that sum of $500,000,000 should have been raised by additional taxation during the period of the war. I do not think there is any foundation for any such statement, and if in the light of what I have said one reviews the financial condition of 1921, one will find-I have not under my hand the figures for more than six years, although I had them at one time-that during the six years prior to my right hon. friend's advent to power, the average annual surplus of the preceding government was $2,000,000 in excess of the surplus which accrued to the government during the first six years of the regime of my right hon. friend. There was something added to the debt, but very much less than would have been added if government had put the whole of the war expenditure into capital. The financing of that period, the carrying on of the vast undertakings of the war has been a creditable page in Canada's history, and my right hon. friend's criticism of it is entirely misleading in that he leaves out that very large amount of capital expenditure which should have been taken into account.
I come now to the speech delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in intro-
The Budget-Mr. Geary

during the budget proposals which are now before the house. In my humble opinion that speech, masterpiece as it was, will stand as a model for budget speeches for many years to come. Not only did the Prime Minister give an exhaustive study and a searching analysis into the conditions, financial and otherwise, of the country, but he enabled us who heard his speech and who had an opportunity of reading it, to understand something of the causes, financially, which have produoed the situation in which we find ourselves to-day. It was an integral part of his presentation; it was the very basis and foundation upon which he built up the case of the country for the increases in taxation which were set out later in the proposals of the same speech.
Former ministers of finance have for many years contented themselves with a recapitulation of the operations of the preceding year, and added to it a statement of their proposals for raising money in addition to certain changes which they proposed to make in the tariff items. It did not occur to them that one of the main features of a budget is the prognostication of the income for the following year, so that when taxes are imposed and changes in the tariff made, there should be presented to the house at the same time a fair estimate of what those changes will bring in, in order that hon. members, in discussing the budget, will have before them an anticipatory result and will know whether they are budgeting simply to cover operating expenses or for an amount which may be used in the reduction of debt. Such a course has not before this year, in my experience, been followed. The result always has been that the minister of finance, although he knew he was budgeting for a surplus, was able to say when the next year came: Here is a pleasant surprise; I have a great surplus and I am reducing the public debt. Similarly in 1930, the then minister of finance, in introducing his budget, must have known quite well that it would result at the end of the year in a substantial deficit. That must have been in his mind, but the election was coming on; the party was going to the country on the basis of that budget, and that budget was designed to omit showing what he well knew must occur, namely, that at the end of the year there would be a substantial deficit.
When the government of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) came into office, they found themselves faced with this huge deficit which was left as a legacy, no matter how one may play upon the word, by the false budgeting of the preceding administration. 
Moreover, the Prime Minister was face to face with the inescapable fact that with existing revenues he would have to have a deficit in the year yet to come. Did he adopt the method of his predecessors? Did he take the easy course-bring down in his proposals, omit to say what his taxation proposals would realize, and then trust to luck at the end of the year, saying probably: We had a deficit; times were hard?. The Prime Minister took the courageous and the only sound business course of determining then and there that the budget of the coming year should balance; that as far as possible there should be sufficient revenue to overcome the expenses which could not be avoided. That resolve met with the commendation of the sound business sense of the country. We have no right at the present moment deliberately to proceed with the coming year's operations in the expectation that at some future time we are going to surmount an enormous deficit. Having arrived at that stage, which I am sure commends itself to the country, my right hon. leader undertook as Minister of Finance to levy the taxation which would be required for the purpose. Long before the house came into session, there was widespread discussion in the country as to what the new taxes would be. It was taken as a foregone conclusion that much more money must be raised. It was realized that the main source from which the additional revenue would come would be some sort of tax on transactions. This took the form of a discussion between an addition to the sales tax and, on the other hand, the imposition of what is known as a turnover tax. I am glad to see the Minister of Finance has adopted the former course and decided to increase to some extent the sales tax which was already upon the statute books. It was a well known tax and its operation was understood. The turnover tax was one which was unfamiliar to all classes of the community. I say that the probability of a deficit was known beforehand by the people and its effect was discounted. For that reason, when the budget came down, that fact being known, the budget, in its proposals, in its review of financial conditions and in all the matters which it contains-I know of none which can be an exception-has met with the approval of all classes of the community. I think that there can be no doubt about that in any way. I have not heard yet, with the exception of a few tariff items, an attack on one single point of the budget that is worthy of the name. The keynote was struck perhaps by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), but it was a faint'

The Budget-Mr. Geary
hearted and weak attack in every respect. I think the hon. gentleman knew very well that he had no ground for his attack, and no better example of it could be found than in the gingerly way in which he touched upon the imposition of the coal duties and entirely omitted, as far as I could see, to make any reference to the steel duties. This was like a red hot poker to him because he comes from a coal and steel country. Anybody who listened to his remarks must, I am sure, have gathered the impression that in truth he is in full accord with the coal taxes as we find them in the budget.
As to the various tariff items, Mr. Speaker, we shall have every opportunity to discuss them when the resolutions are in committee. In this regard the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth largely contented himself with the quoting of some academic remarks from speeches of gentlemen who have lately been meeting in Washington. I do not think it is necessary to discuss that. Whatever general tariff conditions throughout the world may be, they are not of our making. We are met here with a condition and not a theory. We lie next to a country highly developed in industry, protected effectively, and ready to dump its surplus products into this country and destroy our industries. I cannot think that the people of this country for one moment would tolerate any government which will submit this country to a greater degree than it is liable already to the inrush of competition from the United States, let alone of other countries whose markets are not equally open to ours.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth spent most of his time attacking the stand of the Prime Minister in regard to the Canadian National Railways. The hon. member is not present; I wish he were. I would submit to him that he went far out of bis way in a deliberate attempt, or if not deliberate, in a very thinly-disguised attempt, to spread abroad the impression, for party political purposes, that this government is opposed to the Canadian National Railways. I make that statement deliberately. He seemed to base his attack upon a very slim foundation. It was to the effect that in dealing with the sum of $604,000,000, which appears in the accounts as loans from the government, the Prime Minister had conveyed the impression, and as the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth warmed to his work he conveyed the impression that the Prime Minister had deliberately led the house to believe, that this $604,000,000 had all been advanced during the eight years that the Liberal government was in power. Of course that is arrant nonsense. No one was
misled or deceived in that regard. The hon. gentleman said that he himself derived that impression from listening to the speech of the right hon. Minister of Finance. Well, if he did, he knew the facts, and if he were so anxious for a fair presentation of the case of the Canadian National Railways to the public, why did he not by one simple question set the Prime Minister right in that regard, if he were wrong. But he preferred to wait for four days, and gather together a collection of extracts from speeches, brief them and put them into a form where he could argue as an advocate in all the fine ways in which he is trained, in order to deduce the proposition that he was seeking to advance.
I was sorry to see that the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) departed so far from his usual common sense moderation as to join to some extent in the hunt, but I do not think his heart was in it. I do not think for one moment that he would wittingly lend himself to a deliberate attempt on the part of the opposition to convey to the people of Canada the impression that this government was hostile to public ownership and to the Canadian National Railways. Is there anyone in his senses who can find fault with the statement of the Prime Minister in that regard in his budget speech? I am sure that the hon. member for North Waterloo, himself a business man, as a director of one of his companies, would take the very same stand. I would be very much surprised if the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has been drawn into this discussion, does not through its president and directors at the present moment give the closest care and scrutiny to the expenditures and resources of that road. If we could peep behind the scenes I imagine that these gentlemen, who are just as directly confronted with difficulties as we are, would take no other step and no other attitude than that indicated by the Prime Minister in his budget speech as that which this government should take in regard to our own railway.
Outside of that there was a great deal in the speech of the hon. member for North Waterloo with which I agree. This country is committed to public ownership, and it has no regrets on that score. I can speak for my own province from personal knowledge. In Ontario we have embarked on public ownership of different enterprises in many directions, and we have had the greatest satisfaction. There is no body of opinion in Ontario which is opposed to public ownership. I understand that in the city of Montreal the view is not quite the same, and it was not surprising, therefore, to hear the hon. member for Stan-
272S
The Budget-Mr. Geary

stead (Mr. Hackett) giving voice in this chamber not long ago to a view opposed to public ownership. It will serve no useful purpose here and now to enter into a discussion of the relative merits of the two systems. I think it is idle to say that public ownership cannot bring to the management of its enterprises as much skill as can be found by private ownership. The path of private ownership is strewn with financial wrecks. No such casualties as far as I know have occurred in the march of public owrership. I am perfectly satisfied to take my stand, which I believe is that of the rank and file of this party, that public ownership of the national railways is a thing which we do not regret on any score, but is something we are proud of and intend to maintain, and a thing out of which I think this government can make a decided success. Private ownership, of course, is always subjected to the temptation to make returns. That is by no manner of means a condemnation of private ownership. There are great concerns in this country which have been built up on the private ownership principle, and which have devoted themselves to the production of a product at a price that will be fair to the consumers and to the shareholders. Others there are which have not pursued that course. We know to-day of great concerns in this country which have come to grief just because of the greed of those who promoted rather than really owned. The Canadian Pacific Railway, of course, I exempt from any such charge as that. It has been built up on a sure and a proper foundation, and I think we must pay tribute to its management for the skill and business sense, yes, and patriotism, which has characterized its operations. I do not pay that tribute simply to the giants of the past who laid the foundations of and built up that enterprise, but equally to those splendid Canadians, who to-day are in control, particularly its president.
In this country we are bound to have a system of public ownership of railways. There is no regulatory power that can be exercised completely in regard to the rates of railway companies. I think that no board of railway commissioners, however constituted, could effect that result. The only proper regulation of a privately owned railway or of a series of privately owned railways is through a publicly owned enterprise. Competition alone can regulate the rates, and I venture to say that both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway benefit very largely to-day from the incitement of the competition that exists between them. So, Mr. Speaker, I think I am quite safe in say-
ing, and I say it without offence, to my hon. friend from Stanstead, who has a right to his own view, that he is decidedly on the wrong track, and in uttering that view he represents only himself in this house and perhaps a member here and there. Certainly he does not represent in any sense the rank and file of the Conservative party nor, as we heard from the Minister of Fisheries, does he represent in any sense the feeling of the ministry in regard to the Canadian National Railways.
I pass for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to the subamendment moved by the very thoughtful and serious minded member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer). And may I say that amid all the welter of fault finding and recrimination which we have heard from the opposite side of the house I can look only to certain of the hon. members in the far corner for constructive criticism of any sort. Those hon. members have some desire, as is evidenced by their speeches, to cooperate in the governing of the country. The subamendment does seek a way out, and I welcome it, although I think it is premature and with many parts of it I cannot agree. As a whole I do not think it can be substantiated. I shall refer to only one part of the subamendment, namely, the proposal that Canada should abandon the gold standard. One of the reasons given is that under the circumstances which existed in 1914, which are said to be parallel to those existing at the present time, Canada abandoned the gold standard. If, however, circumstances are parallel in any 'particular they are not parallel in the one particular that at that time all gold countries were going off the gold standard; Canada did likewise. At the present time, however, all countries are striving to maintain that standard. The proposal is characteristic of all soft money campaigns. It is a measure of inflation which is designed to produce more currency and credits than are required by the physical needs of industry and trade.

If my hon. friend will
allow me to make a statement, the intention is to allow us to have enough currency to take care of industry and trade. At the present time we have not sufficient.

speechtext:
Supposing we allow a depreciation in currency to the extent of 20 per cent, what is the result? The wheat farmer sells in Great Britain and obtains the currency of that country to the value of SI ,000. That money is returned to Canada and is translated into Canadian dollars. So translated it would bring to the pocket of the farmer $1,250. The inflation that is caused by

The Budget-Mr. Geary
the very act of depreciating our currency designed to raise prices has, in effect, raised prices. So that when we come to the point of spending that $1,250 at the stabilized price level we get for that $1,250 at the higher price level just as many articles as we would have received for the $1,000 at the previous level. That seems to be perfectly sound reasoning.
