speechtext: I would like to remind the hon. member that outside the value of commodities there is the very important factor of the increase in our .public and private debts to an abnormal extent by the recent drastic deflation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is a branch of the subject I had not mentioned. My hon. friend has in mind the fallacy that in regard to debt reduction the inflation of currency would help. That is attacking however by an unsound financial method a problem of an entirely different sort, and it does not seem to me that the two can be intermingled. To admit, as I think we are bound, that this depreciation is an unsound method of finance, and then say that it may apply to some other conditions, I think is quite beside the point. The statement is made that Australia has benefited by a withdrawal from the gold standard. I have seen no evidence to show that Australia has benefited in any degree whatsoever. The Australian farmer may receive three shillings whereas the Canadian farmer will receive only fifty cents. If however the farmer in Australia receives three shillings, under the price levels existing in Australia to-day that three shillings will not buy him as much of the commodities he desires to have as will the fifty cents of the Canadian farmer. May I throw out the suggestion that the Canadian farmer is not concerned with the price of a bushel of wheat, but with the exchange value. I can see that the exchange value would not be increased in the slightest degree by a deliberate inflation or depreciation of our currency. I do not suggest that my argument disposes entirely of the proposal. I do say however that there are considerations which certainly should be examined with great care. I hardly think my hon. friend would expect his proposal to gain the support of all hon. members in the house, but his suggestion offers a matter for discussion. I know my hon. friend will give quotations from the works of eminent economists in support of his proposal. I am equally aware of the fact however that just as many, and manv more, economists can be found who
will say that the proposal of my hon. friend is not sound.
May I however in passing tell the hon. member for Battle River to be of good cheer. His subamendment is not yet lost. Remember the days of the subamendment to the debate on the address. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition may well find that the exigencies of the occasion justify him and his followers-at least those of his followers who will follow him-to vote for my hon. friend's amendment to the amendment. My right hon. friend may find, as he found once before, that the good blue pencil is the best weapon after all. He may find that after striking out all the words after "whereas" in the amendment he will be just as ready to vote for it as for the amendment, if by that action he may get the support of the hon. members in the corner of the house. Although my right hon friend may be a bit censorious, as I indicated, he may have the desire once more to effect a juncture in the voting power of the two groups opposite me in the chamber. As I look back on the debate on the address the et tu Brute of my right hon. friend rings in my ears. My right hon. friend who used to refer to the hon. members in the corner of the house as "Liberals in a hurry" had lost their support, but apparently at the time of the debate on the address he desired a rapprochement. As I say, after the vote on the address he turned upon them in a censorious manner and, as he believed, set my hon. friends in the far corner exactly in their places. However, the two opposing groups are together in some particulars; they both indulge somewhat in counsels of despair. We have been told by the hon. ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that we are prophets, major and minor. He is right; we are if you like, prophets, major and minor. So far as Canada is concerned we are prophets of faith, hope and courage. We do not follow the counsels of despair we hear from other parts of the house. We know that there is distress in all parts of Canada, but we do not purpose to lie down and do nothing. We are going to assume the burden. To use another simile we are going to take the labouring oar and fight the matter out. We do not assume the attitude of our hon. friends opposite who send a greeting from the one to the other across the abyss of interrupted friendship which might be expressed in the words:
Welcome kindred gloom
Congenial horrors hail.
We, on this side of the house will fight it out and find the remedy.
The Budget-Mr. Geary

My hon. friends opposite seem to be very much concerned about the attitude of this government in regard to unemployment. All that can be done in regard to unemployment will be done. The example given in the past by this government has shown that it can do, and is prepared to do and will do, more than any other previous government has tried to do.
Its record shows that it can do, and will dlo more than any other government has ever tried to do on behalf of the unemployed. Contrast this attitude towards unemployment with the attitude of my hon. friends opposite just a year ago, when they put up their Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) to declare that whatever unemployment existed had to do only with seasonal occupations, and when in fact they derided the existence of unemployment, and took no measures to relieve it. But, to-day they admit there is unemployment, and they demand that this government, whose members then recognized there was unemployment and today are doing their very best to afford relief, should not be entrusted to take such measures to deal with the problem as may from time to time be necessary. That there is no declaration in the budget of any policy in regard to unemployment is no indication that the government will do nothing. On the contrary, their record so far is an assurance that they will do their utmost to solve the problem, and indeed we have the statement of a member of the cabinet that the matter is occupying their attention day by day, that they are giving it most sympathetic and careful attention, aware of the distress and determined to see to its relief. I think we can trust this government, as we could not trust a government composed of hon. members opposite, to effect a solution of this difficulty.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) looks to be a successful and prosperous businessman, as I believe he is, but to my great surprise he advanced the proposition that we should not impose taxes to balance our national accounts; on the contrary, that we should let them become a capital charge; and to my greater surprise still, many hon. members on the other side of the house applauded that sentiment, with the notable exception of the right hon. leader of the opposition and the former hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe); they sat silent as the tomb. I think they must have writhed inwardly when they heard that suggestion. They must haye thought of the many occasions on which they have boasted

of the action of their Minister of Finance, Mr. Fielding, in 1922. Boasted of what? Of the fact that to meet the deficit which was sure to come he imposed new taxation, for he declared that the first requisite of sound financial administration was to balance the budget. Is it any wonder that my right hon. friend opposite could not applaud the statement of the hon. member for Sherbrooke? To-day history repeats itself. Then the vast effort of this country in the war, the providing of pensions, and the expenditures necessary for railway rehabilitation required a large addition to the public debt, and also to the amount of money to meet the annual outgo. To-day this government finds itself heir to an enormous deficit left by its evicted predecessors. In those days Mr. Fielding refused to accept responsibility in regard to revenues and expenditures for a year during only part of which he had been in office; to-day we find the same situation. Then the government of the day decided to balance the budget; to-day the same course is being taken. Then it became necessary to impose new taxation; to-day we find ourselves under the same impelling necessity. The taxes, strangely enough, that were imposed by the government of the right hon. leader of the opposition-which I hope he will remember-were, in essence, the same sort of taxes that are being imposed to-day. Then there was a sales tax. Mr. Fielding in 1922 raised that by one-half, and next year he raised it to six per cent. We are raising it from one to four per cent-not nearly to the point he raised it.
We have been chidden to some extent by hon. members opposite for our motions of the last two or three sessions to abolish the sales tax. We were perfectly right; the sales tax should have been abolished when we moved those resolutions. It was retained long after the necessity for it had passed. When the government of the day was amassing large surpluses and there was no further need of a sales tax, that tax was continued for the purpose of swelling the revenues and enabling the finance minister of the day to boast a surplus. At that time he also increased the "nuisance" taxes. Beyond the tariff increases I know of nothing we are doing to-day that they were not doing at that time. Perhaps that is the reason there has been no attack of any consequence made upon the proposals.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say what I am afraid is merely a repetition, that the people have got some sense, they are not ignorant of the conditions that confront the government. They know that we fell heir to

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
this legacy of debt, they know that proper business principles impel us to wipe off all that debt, and they are not of opinion that it should be wiped off by charging the deficit to capital account. And because we have taken a bold and courageous course, not letting things ride, to use a .colloquialism, for another year, but facing the situation and fighting it out, for the very reason that the people admire a fighting man they are behind the Prime Minister in his efforts in that regard. Whatever one may say of the tariff proposals -and they are proper matters for discussion- I think we can close this debate resting perfectly assured that although the people do not like to pay taxes, they have enough sense to know, and do know, that this government is imposing taxes in the proper and only way in which under the -circumstances they should be imposed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have forty minutes in which to deal with the budget, the amendment to the budget, and the amendment to the amendment. Everyone knows that that is an impossibility. I must therefore confine myself to particular phases of the motion and the two amendments. First I shall deal with the subamendment and endeavour to answer the arguments put forth by those who have found it necessary to disagree with us in that regard.
With respect to the subamendment, may I say in the first place that it affords us an opportunity to protest against certain items in the budget to which we take exception. There is no other provision under the party system foy which we can make an intelligent protest against anything that we might disagree with in the budget. Later I shall refer specifically to some of those matters on which we disagree with the government. In the preamble of our amendment we have indicated our conviction that there must of necessity take place fundamental changes in the economic system before we can expect to be relieved of the depression and human suffering with which we are surrounded at the present. We indicate, further, the course to be pursued and the goal of our reform, namely, cooperation for the highest human values, rather than competition for profit. Recognizing that to remodel the entire economic system of the nation will require a great deal of thought, a great deal of planning, and a great deal of time, we have put forward a specific proposal which we thought would bring some immediate relief to the people. That specific proposal, as everyone knows, is the proposal to suspend the redemption of dominion notes in gold-not necessarily to suspend such redemption forever, although I would very
gladly do that; we suggest nothing more at the present time than a temporary suspension of that redemption.
Now, to deal with these three things separately. Let me say before I take them up in detail that there may be some question as to our tactics in moving an amendment at this time. Indeed, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) did take exception to our tactics and charged us with playing party politics. I am afraid I shall have to agree to a considerable extent with my right hon. friend in that regard; not that we designedly played party politics, but that being in a party institution it is just as difficult to stay here without playing politics as it would be to fall into the sea and come out without getting wet. I agree with him to this extent, that in moving the amendment to the budget we have adopted heretofore the party psychology. I frankly tell the house that I personally am opposed t-o the party psychology. Let me read the motion which is before the house. It is: that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of ways and means. That is the motion.
I suggest that in future all independent members who are dissociated from the major parties of the house should adopt a different policy entirely in dealing with the budget. We should vote for the motion to go into committee, as the motion proposes, and if there be anything in the budget with which we do agree, when the resolutions reach the committee stage we should take the opportunity of moving an amendment to every specific item from which we dissent. By taking that course we should escape from the party entanglements which always lie in wait for an independent member in connection with the budget vote, and at the same time we should be able to vote on specific issues, disentangling them from the tremendous mass of issues of which every budget is composed. .
Let me give to the house an example of the absurdity with which I am personally faced at the moment. And I shall take only one example out of a hundred. I am asked by one vote to decide whether or not I want the five cents a bushel bonus on wheat; and on the other hand I am asked to decide whether or not I am in favour of the reduction in income tax on higher incomes. Now, frankly, I am in favour of the five cent bonus on wheat, and I should like to vote for it. But I am decidedly opposed to the reduction of the income tax on higher incomes and I want to vote against it. But I have only one vote. I am asked to vote yes or no; I want
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

to vote yes and no. I hope that the independent groups in parliament will from this time take such a course as will free their own minds from this absurdity and give us an opportunity to vote on issues on their merits.
Let me come now to the various parts of our amendment which I enumerated a few moments ago. I shall deal first with our conviction that the economic system requires some modifications. Let me point out, what perhaps it is scarcely necessary to indicate to this assembly, that events are demonstrating more and more clearly each day the necessity for some fundamental changes in our economic system. Let me present to this house the actual condition with which we are faced, having regard also to the amendment which we have moved.
The more we produce the less we consume in relation to the output. The more goods that are produced and unconsumed, the more unemployment; the more unemployment the greater distress and depression; and the more distress and depression the greater and more imminent is the danger to society. Now let us follow out the reasoning of these propositions.
Production under the capitalistic system is undertaken only for profit. To make a profit goods must be sold for more money than was expended in their production; otherwise there can be no profit. Now let us take the national output or the output of the world. Some of my hon. friends like to talk about the world. Very well; let us take the world or the nation, whichever you choose. The national or world output of goods, it is obvious, cannot all be sold for more than was expended in their production. Therefore under a profit system they cannot all be sold. There must remain a surplus, to buy which there is no money in circulation. That surplus forms the basis of unemployment, and unemployment is measured by that surplus in every country of the world. Briefly, then, this is the reason why the present policies of both major parties in this house must inevitably fail in the ultimate.
The party opposite, now in office, stands for more production, more factories-a splendid ambition if we were in a position to reap the benefit of this increased production. But since the people cannot buy what is already produced, it will not help them to know that there is still more produced which they cannot buy. There is no comfort in that. Since unemployment is caused by the surplus which cannot be sold, more production which cannot be sold will cause still more unemployment.

Then turn to the other party. It argues that if trade between nations were freer we should be able to trade ourselves out of unemployment and into prosperity-rather a novel conception. This I regard as a doubleheaded fallacy, because every other nation is as helpless and as hopeless to buy goods as we are, and for precisely the same reason. Moreover, there is in almost every civilized country of the world, a surplus of the very goods of which we have a surplus. That is not absolutely true in detail, but I say that in the main, and in respect of civilized countries, it is true. There are no foreign markets, and if there were foreign markets, foreign markets would not increase purchasing power of the countries concerned. Foreign trade properly considered is only fair exchange, purchasing power remaining the same in both the bargaining countries.
Now, it was with a view to increasing temporarily the purchasing power of the country, thus relieving the pressure in Canada, that we proposed to suspend the redemption of dominion notes in gold. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) argued very ably and very clearly this whole subject. I can only touch upon it, there being so many other matters to which I must refer. I have argued this subject many times in this house. The very first speech I ever made on this floor was on this subject. At that time I warned the then government that they should not be tempted to go back on the gold basis, pointing out to them that to do so at that time would very materially increase the debts, both personal and public. I showed that it would place agriculture in particular under a burden from which it would be very doubtful whether it would ever emerge. I can remember the scoffs which came from the government benches on that occasion.
I am glad to note that ten years later the right hon. leader of the opposition, then the Prime Minister, thinks enough of our proposals to take a little time to argue against them. That marks at least some advance. In his speech of great length and breadth, which necessarily yielded some of its depth to the other two dimensions, the right hon. leader of the opposition gave some attention to the subamendment. He spoke favourably, if vaguely, with regard to international cooperation. That is all very well, but we want cooperation in Canada. I would stand for cooperation in Canada if there were not another nation in the world wanting cooperation. If it should take all the nations of the world all time to become cooperatives, I do not want Canada to wait that long. It is all

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
very well to talk about international cooperation when there does not exist one international body in the world possessed either of the idea of cooperation or the authority to take the first step in that direction. We have no power, either, to bring the other nations of the world into cooperative action, and therefore I say for the right hon. leader of the opposition to place the seal of his endorsation upon international cooperation is merely to make an appeal to the empty sky.
I ask, then, for cooperation in Canada. Russia used to think that her communism could not be established unless it were done by international revolution, and I venture to say she spent a good many months and years trying to incite the other nations of the world to revolt, and thus to carry out her program. Eventually she discovered that if she were to have communism she would have to have it in Russia and leave the rest of the world to mind its own business. I do not argue that we should ignore the rest of the world, but I do say that our best contribution to international cooperation can be made only by building up cooperation In Canada. I want cooperation in Canada in the production of goods; I want cooperation in the distribution of goods; I want cooperation in farming; I want cooperation in finance; I want cooperation between the working people of this country and the bankers and financiers. If we cannot get that kind of cooperation then the principle of cooperation must be thrown overboard. I refuse, however, to wait for that cooperation until it is established internationally. We must begin at home.
The leader of the opposition apparently was unable to see any benefit in our next proposal, which was to renounce the gold standard. I agree with him, however, in his criticism that the advantage which might be gained by a country going off the gold basis is very largely lost-though not entirely, as he claimed-when other countries take the same action. I agree with that part of his criticism, but he forgets that we are now suffering from a disadvantage because our competitors in the world's markets have already gone off the gold basis. Thus the only possible way we can have even a fair chance with them is to have our monetary system at least upon a basis comparable to theirs. So the primary objeot in moving the amendment in this connection is, in short, that we may be placed on a fair basis with other countries competing with us.
Let me put it in another way: we want to abandon the gold basis for a reason similar to that which made the Liberal party continue a protectionist policy through a long regime
in office; that is, in order to adjust ourselves to our competitors. That is not all that would result from such a proposal, however. It would decidedly reduce debt. Just as debt was increased in Canada when we went on the gold basis, so debt would be reduced in exactly the same way by getting off the gold basis. I say to this parliament that this government and members of this house owe it to justice and to the people of Canada to inflate now to the same extent that deflation took place under the previous government after the war. When, as I have often said in this house, the debt of every farmer, and the national debt, was more than doubled. That occurred in this way, that it took two bushels of wheat, two hours of labour or two units of any other sort to do what one unit could have done prior to the deflation. That is how it increased our debt.
In substance, the right hon. leader of the opposition argued.that if there had been any intention to go off the gold basis, provision should have been made for that action before refinancing took place. I think the inference is that it would be unfair to bondholders for us to go off the gold basis now, after they have reinvested and have been reassured of the gilt-edged character of their investments. It was very unfortunate for the people of Canada that my right hon. friend did not see that point when he was in power; he deliberately went on to the gold basis, thus placing a burden upon the people of Canada which would be in part placed upon the bondholders if we were to do the reverse now. The unfairness on that occasion was directed against the general public, and the unfairness on this occasion would be against the bondholders, but since the bondholders already have reaped their advantage by deflation, the general public should have a chance to get squared by an equal measure of inflation.
To abandon the gold basis is, of course, frankly admitted to be against the interests of bondholders. To return to the gold basis was against the interests of the masses of the people. My right hon. friend betrayed his millionaire psychology through his own eloquence. Is it not amusing that in the same speech in which he so properly, and with such deep emotion, condemned the government for having reduced the income tax on the higher incomes, he should have rushed to the defence of the bondholders with breast bared to the enemy? Yes, the abandonment of the gold basis would reduce the incomes of bondholders, and so the right hon. leader of the opposition rushes to defend them. What law of justice or of economics; what rule of ethics permits the right hon. gentleman to arrive at the conclusion that it is a good policy to
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

defend the interests of the bondholders as against the very life of the Canadian people, the wage earners, the farmers and the merchants of this country? The price of wheat may decrease to the vanishing point; the debt of the farmers, by deflation, may be heaped up to twice its original size; the wage earner, through deflation, may go on short time and thus reduce his income, or eventually he may be thrown out of employment and have no income at all; the bread winners of Canada may not be able to provide for their families and there may be hungry children in this country, but that did not seem to arouse the sympathies of the right hon. leader of the opposition when he was in power. Now, however, he is aroused by the mere suggestion that we should reduce the interest and consequently the profit on bonds. Should not the wage eaner, the farmer, the hungry children of Canada, have a status in this parliament equal to that of. the bondholders? I venture to suggest to the right hon. leader of the opposition and to the bondholders that the time has come when bondholders must bear their share of the burden of depression and distress which our false financial system has placed upon the country. No longer is it possible to defend a situation which thrusts all the suffering resulting from a faulty economic system upon the masses of the people-people such as walked up the front steps of this building yesterday demanding work or the hundreds who sleep on the dumps of the cities or the hundreds of thousands throughout the Dominion of Canada who must have charity or starve. If we are passing through a world depression for which no individual is responsible, then all classes in Canada must be prepared to bear their share of that burden.
I come now to the amendment which contains a lot of "whereases," a lot of regrets and a number of platitudes. Those are the three divisions of the amendment. I shall not deal with the "whereases," although some of them are inaccurate. I shall not trouble with the regrets, because regrets produce no results. I shall comment on the platitudes, because sometimes platitudes do a great deal more harm than good. Under the division of platitudes, the amendment reads:
That the existing economic depression can only be overcome by policies which are of a character,
(a)	to relieve unemployment,
(b)	to restore to a condition of parity the relation between the purchasing powers of all classes,
(c)	to bring about more equitable distribution of the burdens of taxation.,
(d)	to encourage the expansion of the external trade of the country.

Supposing a doctor said to a patient suffering from insomnia: The way to cure insomnia is to accept treatment which will restore natural sleep to you, my man; or if he should say to another: The way to relieve the hungry from the pangs of hunger is to give them food -everybody knows that. That is analogous to the platitudinous attempt of the opposition to make the people think they have made a fruitful proposal. They have made no proposals; they have said what everybody would say and nobody would disagree with, and it does not matter whether it is said or not. There is not a word in the amendment as to how all these good things are to be accomplished. Of course it is intended that the house and the country should presume that the policies of the Liberal party will supply all these things, but there is a long record of deeds to nullify the presumption. If the last ten budgets brought down by the former Liberal government had contained policies such as "to relieve unemployment," "to restore parity of purchasing power," to "equalize taxation," and to "expand foreign trade," there obviously would have been no need for this amendment at this time. But unfortunately for Canada, and perhaps for the Liberal party, they brought down all these budgets without including any policies of such a character as would produce those results. So we are led to reflect upon what might have been. That recalls to mind these lines:
For of all sad words of tongue or pen,
The saddest are these: "It might have been!"
In further criticism the leader of the opposition proceeded to deal with what I would call the Liberal theory of relativity of trade. I have no time to expose in detail what I regard as the fallacies of that position, but I want to answer it in a manner which I think will be sufficient for my present purpose. All the house remembers what the leader of the opposition contended with regard to the relativity of the natural conditions in a country producing the same kind of goods, so that a jack-knife produced in the Argentine traded for a jack-knife produced in Canada, is the proper way to trade, and we ought to welcome it. That is, of course, my characterization of his position. But let me follow that up. Let me assume the absence of all tariff barriers in Canada. Let me assume the internationalism about which my right hon. friend speaks. In short, let me. assume "the federation of the world and the parliament of man," and the leader of the opposition as prime minister. I should like to ask him whether, under those conditions, we would not still have unemployment. He would then add the unemploy-

ment of Europe to the unemployment of Canada and the unemployment of the north American continent to that of the orient, and he would have exactly the same problem now under a prime minister of the world as we have in Canada under a national prime minister, because merely extending the boundary does not at all increase the purchasing power. Unfortunately, however, I must leave the consideration of that in order to deal with the budget itself.
The high compliments which have been paid to the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) for the comprehensiveness of the budget and for the lucidity of his presentation of the business affairs of the country have been well merited. I should like very briefly to point out in respect to the budget the few things with which I agree and to conclude with the things with which I do not agree. First I wish to commend the government for having provided a five cent a bushel bonus on wheat. It is not enough, we say, but five cents a bushel will be a little increase to the purchasing power of the farmers of western Canada in particular, and everybody who knows anything about the situation, realizes that that will be of great value. But of even greater value than that is the implication that from now on, if tariff policies are to be persisted with, there must be compensation for agriculture for the extra burden which the tariff imposes. The leader of the opposition called this bonus a sop. Let me remind him that for many years he maintained a very high tariff and never even gave a sop. In this matter I declare my view that the government is to be commended on giving this. I am going to tell the government later why it should not be commended for not doing other things. Next I say that the government did well when it imposed a tax upon income from foreign capital. That was another very good thing to do. It did good work also when it increased the income tax in a certain division, shall I say? I shall deal with the other divisions later. But from, I think $3,500 to $130,000 or so there has been an increase in the income tax which will bring a greater revenue to the country than previously. For these things especially I feel that the government ought properly to be commended.
But let me now turn to the other phases of the budget with which I do not agree, and I think the outstanding one is the reduction in the income tax on the higher income. I agree entirely with the leader of the opposition on this point; I think his forceful criticism in this respect was well taken. Let me say in all friendliness to the government:	I
The Budget-Mr. Irvine
do not think you can afford to do it. It really does not make very much difference to the income after all. There may not be many people who will be affected by this alteration, but if there be one or, as the leader of the opposition says, even if there is not one, the very fact of the willingness on the part of the government to make this alteration is an unfortunate psychological condition. In view also of the fact that there are in the ranks of the governing party men who may have a little bit more money than I have,-this may be doubtful, but some may have a little more-do not give the public a chance to say that you are trying to protect your own necks by this petty reduction. Put this item back on the old schedule. I hope the government will do this. In fact, I noted when the Minister of Finance was making his speech, if I recall it aright, he said he had taken this item exactly as it was presented to him by the officials of the department. That statement may be regarded as leaving the back door open, and I sincerely hope that before the budget is passed he and his government will go out of that back door, taking the reduction objected to along with them.
I want next to oppose the change in the stamp tax on cheques. The ten dollar limit has been removed. Let me point out to the government that this tax falls very heavily indeed upon the farmers, who deal in small milk cheques, egg cheques and butter cheques. Many of these cheques amount to only sixty cents apiece, and on that sixty cents they must pay two cents. I know that the government will argue that the purchaser of the farmers' goods will pay the stamp tax. Yes, but ultimately he charges that back in reduced prices to the farmers who sell the goods. Whether he does so or not, let me tell you that the farmers believe that he does. For all the extra money that this change in the tax will bring, I think there ought to be modification. At least limit it to cheques over five dollars. Let me suggest another change. Charge four cents on every cheque over thirty dollars, and in that way you will perhaps get more money than you will lose by exempting cheques up to five dollars.
I come to the last point of disagreement, and that is with respect to unemployment. I think all members so far have regretted that there has been no definite policy announced by the government in respect to unemployment relief. I am not entirely convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the budget is the proper place to bring forward a program of relief for unemployment. I think that it is not

if for no other reason than this, that no one knows just how many millions of dollars are going to be required to take eare of unemployment during the next year. But when I say that, I say this also, that I do not think this parliament should prorogue until the government has clearly announced what its policy in this respect will be and the necessary legislation has been provided to enable it to carry that policy into effect. I am in hopes that the government has no other intention than to do that, and so I am not going to criticize it for not doing what 1 cannot believe it will not do.
In respect to the relief of unemployment let me emphasize one or two constructive suggestions, whether they are so regarded or not. I would lay it down as the first principle of relief that every man, woman and child in Canada who is in want through unemployment must receive adequate food, clothing and shelter. That is the first principle for us to lay down, and this government must accept the responsibility therefor.
Next I would suggest that in order to provide these necessities we should organize in all the larger centres of Canada, bureaus for the distribution for free food and free clothing to all registered unemployed, and that such food and clothing shall be purchased in Canada, that food such as butter, eggs, and bread shall be purchased from the farmers of this country, and the clothing and boots shall be bought from our Canadian factories, and that in accepting that responsibility we shall see to it that our people receive at least a bare living from the industries of the country. Less than that we cannot do.
I would suggest also that the committee or board suggested by the right hon. leader of the opposition might be a very good means of carrying into effect the proposals which I have just made.
As to the solution for unemployment, that is a very different .question. I never have thought that any modification of the tariff would cure unemployment. That is one reason why we do not mention the tariff in our amendment. We know perfectly well that it will hot effect a cure either for unemployment or for the economic difficulties of agriculture. Let me give an example of the problem which unemployment involves. According to an article in MacLean's Magazine last summer, at the end of 1931 there will be released in Canada sufficient horse-power from the development of hydro-electrical energy alone to do the work of 50,000,000 men. That is only one single .phase of the industrial system. It must be clear that by substituting solar

energy and mechanical appliances for the muscular power of men we have very, very materially increased our powers of production, and thus reduced the necessity for man power. There is the crux of the problem. But the problem cannot be solved by maintaining the same system. There is no hope of finding an outlet- for our products in other countries, as the leader of the opposition suggested. There was a time in the history of capitalism when a large portion of the world was unexploited, and when to seek markets in other countries had some meaning, but aft this stage of capitalism, when the entire world has been exploited, there is no possibility of finding relief through foreign markets for our surplus production. So I say that, in order to meet the problem which I have just tried! to illustrate by that one statement of fact, we must take a course cooperative in nature which will make the industries of Canada keep the people of Canada, instead of the people of Canada keeping the industries of Canada. We shall discover from year to year as we go along accepting responsibility for unemployment, that the only source from which we can draw to carry out that obligation is our industries, and ultimately we shall have to take over our industries or put them on a cooperative basis in order to secure the necessary supplies.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I believe that the evidences of the age in which we 'live, and the great events with which w7e are faced, clearly demonstrate that we are passing out of the old competitive capitalistic system into a new. But the great problem is, how shall it be accomplished? What method shall be followed? One class of people says: We will do it by revolution. Another class says: We will do it by evolution. Another class says: We do not require to do it at all because this old system, praise God, is eternal. Those are the three conditions of mind of the people of Canada alt the present time. Revolution, to my mind, is the way of distress and ignorance, but it is inevitable if we are going to have a class of people who will persist in maintaining that there is no need of any modifications. If we are going to effect the change from the competitive system to the cooperative system by evolutionary process, it is necessary that we recognize responsibility in the evolutionary process. Responsibility for the evolutionary process cannot be exercised or discharged simply by sitting quietly and doing nothing. We must plan for evolution. If we would escape the disaster that hangs over the world at the present time we must first come to the conviction that modifications of the present

The Budget-Mr. Veniot
system are inevitable, and then we must plan how to make those modifications with the least possible dislocation and the least possible human suffering. I hope that the cooperation which has been suggested by the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Geary) and by other hon. members of this house will ultimately take possession of this parliament. Who knows how to fix up this unemployed question? Not one of us. Why should we try to make political capital out of our economic blundering with its unavoidable suffering?
I would characterize the amendment of my right hon. friend to my night as a drag net cast into the sea of our discontent in the hope of gathering therefrom party advantage. This is not a time when we can dare to tamper with a situation of this kind. I plead with the government and with the parties in the house, I plead with the moneyed men of this country, the bondholders, the bankers, and the employers, that we are sitting on a volcano and nothing but cooperative intelligence will save the situation.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to contribute my quota to the debate on the budget, I wish first to extend my congratulations to my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the very able, interesting, eloquent and forceful enunciation of Liberal principles made by him last night. I have been a Liberal all my life; in the thirty-five years that I have been in active public service I have never seen any reason why I should be otherwise. I have been proud of being a Liberal, but never was I so proud as last night when I heard my right hon. leader enunciate the principles of the Liberal party.
Before I undertake to discuss the budget, I wish for a short time to pay my respects to the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. McDade). I may say that I was amused and somewhat surprised to hear my hon. friend in his maiden speech express the good feelings he had towards your humble servant in one breath and in the next breath make a personal attack against me. I hope that my young friend will come to learn that tactics of that kind are better left aside, especially when we are dealing with the important questions that are before the house 22110-174
and the country to-day. I am sure, sir, that on sober second thought he will realize how far such an exaggerated sense of ego as has characterized his speeches lately may, if not restrained, lead him into the realm of absurdity. In his personal attack on me the hon. gentleman referred to the reduction of the usual majority which for a long number of years I obtained in the county I have the honour to represent in this house, and he said that the handwriting was on the wall. Let me say to my hon. and juvenile friend from the county of Northumberland that at the next election there will be no "handwriting on the wall" so far as he is concerned, but the rattling of the bones of the political skeleton will remind him of the violated pledges made by himself and by his leader during the campaign last July.
Instead of taking up the time of the house to deal with election matters in the county of Gloucester, it would have been far better for my hon. friend had he undertaken to explain to the people in his county why he is supporting such a high tax on gasoline. If there is one county in the province of New Brunswick where gasoline is used to a very, very large extent it is the county that my hon. friend has the honour of representing in this house. And the fishermen of Northumberland are certainly not regarding with any great favour the imposition of this tax upon the gasoline which they are using in so many ways in carrying on their business and earning their daily bread.
It would have better suited the people of Northumberland county if my young friend had taken up the time of this house to discuss the question of the extra duty on tin plate. In the county of Northumberland and the other northern sections of New Brunswick, including the county of Westmorland, tin plate is used very extensively in the canning of fish. There reside in the county of my hon. friend two of the largest fish packers in the maritime provinces. Yet he had not one word of protest to make in this house against the imposition of the higher tax on tin plate. Why, if he thought of tin plate at all, did he not enter a protest not only against the imposition of that tax, but against the discrimination made in freight rates on tin plate from the Ojibway factory,-a factory established in the interests of the United States Steel Corporation-in favour of those centres in Ontario where fruit and vegetables are canned? The discrimination is against the maritime provinces. We are called upon today to pay 20 per cent more for the transportation of tin plate from Ojibway to the

Yet my hon. friend preferred to take up the time of this house in making his attack upon the member for Gloucester rather than demonstrate to the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) the injustice that has been done to the people of the county that he represents and to the people of the county that I represent.

speechtext:
It was not my place to go to the railway commission and attempt to influence them. I am now laying the matter before the house, and I would ask the right hon. Minister of Finance to take it up with the railway commission and see that this discrimination against the maritime provinces is discontinued.
There is another question that the hon. gentleman might have dealt with which is of immediate importance to the people of his county, and that is the sales tax on rope for fishing nets and lobsters traps. These articles were exempt in the past. To-day under this budget they no longer enjoy that exemption, yet the hon. member for Northumberland never raised his voice in protest. Before the introduction of the budget the sales tax on our fish goods was only one half per cent. Today salmon, sardines and other canned fish are subject to a sales tax of four per cent. Yet in this case too, the hon. gentleman coming from a county where a lot of this foodstuff is canned has not deigned to raise his voice in protest or to ask the government to look into the matter.
During his speech, in a voice filled with emotion, the hon. member asked this question: What has the Liberal government ever done for the maritime provinces? I regret, Mr. Speaker, that in his first speech in this house the hon. gentleman has displayed such a want of knowledge of the political history of his own province and of the maritimes generally. For his information, and for the information of other maritime members, permit me to place on Hansard a list of what the Liberal government has done for the maritime provinces.
It was under a Liberal government that the maritime provinces were given a 20 per

cent reduction in freight rates, which put into the pockets of the people no less a sum than about $3,000,000 a year.
It was under Liberal rule that the maritimes received two increases in provincial subsidy, one in 1907-and for the province of New Brunswick this meant $130,000 a year-and the other in 1928, the latter amounting, for the three maritime provinces, to about $1,500,000.
It was under Liberal rule that Prince Edward Island obtained additional transportation facilities, which have so greatly aided in the development of the resources of that island. And it was under Liberal rule that the present Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) was enabled to enjoy a trip to Levis a few weeks ago to inspect the new ferry boat which the Liberal government put under construction to aid the people of Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Were not all these recommendations of the Duncan commission?

No matter what they were, we gave them to the people of the maritime provinces. And let me observe that the hon gentleman opposed the Duncan commission when it was first proposed.
It was under Liberal rule that Nova Scotia and New Brunswick received for the first time a subvention to extend their coal trade further west; and this was in addition to the 20 per cent general reduction in freight rates already referred to.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Everything done under pressure.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, but in spite of the
opposition of hon. gentlemen opposite, who expressed the view that the appointment of the Duncan commission was a farce.

speechtext:
Because we knew what the
country wanted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Take your medicine. My
hon. friends do not like this. It was under Liberal rule that these things were accomplished. May I suggest, before I proceed, that if these hon. gentlemen cannot bear to hear these truths they are at liberty to go out.
It was under Liberal rule that the Nova Scotia coal industry received a bonus of 49 cents a ton on coal manufactured into coke for metallurgical purposes, which placed the Sydney steel industry on an equal footing with the Algoma steel works and the Canada Steel Corporation, who were receiving a drawback of 99 per cent on American coal which they were using for the same purposes. And

it was because of that subvention that certain members from the maritime provinces, notably from the Sydneys, voted against their own party and in favour of the Liberal policy in 1930.

They were returned
in July.

speechtext:
I am not labouring; I am
stating facts and they do not appear to please hon. gentlemen. It was under Liberal rule that an additional 10 per cent preference was given on all British goods imported through Canadian ports, which action greatly aided the development of trade through the ports of St. John and Halifax, and practically shut out imports through Portland. Let me add that prior to the granting of this 10 per cent for the purpose of assisting maritime ports, large quantities of goods were imported from Great Britain into Canada through American ports, and within a year of the granting of that 10 per cent preference 991 per cent of all British goods came through the maritime ports and through the port of Montreal.
It was under Liberal rule that the harbours of Halifax and St. John were put under commission.
It was under Liberal rule that there was adopted a plan involving the expenditure of $11,000,000 to improve the port of St. John, and also a plan for the expenditure of large sums for improvements in the port of Halifax.
It was under Liberal rule that the great railway works were established in Moncton and the attempt was frustrated to have Moncton side tracked.
It was under Liberal rule that a line of steamships was established between the maritime provinces and the British West Indies, which has been so successful in increasing the business of the ports of St. John and Halifax.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has it been a success financially?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It will be if you give it
time. It was under Liberal rule that the Valley railroad was taken over and the province of New Brunswick relieved of a bonded indebtedness of $6,000,000.
It was under Liberal rule that the Kent Northern, the Albert Southern and the St. Martins railways were taken over by the Canadian National Railways in those sections, and the province given better service.
The Liberal government was the first to give special reduced freight rates on potatoes from the east to the west to open up a larger market for the potato growers of the maritime provinces. It was under Liberal rule that the subsidy was granted for the construction of coke plants to encourage the manufacture of coke from Canadian coal. A subvention or subsidy, whatever you choose to call it, was given of 4 per cent on the cost price of the plants wherever established in Canada. Besides that, in order to encourage further the manufacture of coke in the maritime provinces, the Liberal government gave a subvention of 5 per cent of the cost of any plants that might be erected by any municipality or city in the maritime provinces.
The hon. member for Northumberland also referred to the regulations recently adopted by the Department of Fisheries in connection with salmon fishing, and he intimated that I had attempted to take credit for any change made in these regulations. No man has ever heard my voice raised in this house or out of it at any time to take credit for anything I may have accomplished in that line. I was the first and only member from the province of New Brunswick to take the matter up in the house. I called the attention of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) to what I knew was, and what my people represented to me to be, a grave injustice in the adoption of these new regulations. The minister was kind enough to say that a man would be sent to the province of New Brunswick to look further into the matter. It is true the deputy minister did go to the province, and he was accompanied, I understand, by the hon. member for Northumberland. While I am free to admit that the deputy minister would not in any way attempt to make politics out of the matter, I am convinced that the hon. member for Northumberland accompanied him with no other object in view than to make political capital and try to show the people he was doing something for them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Of course you would not do anything like that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should have to live in
York-Sunbury, represented by my hon. friend, to learn how to do that. He knows the trick so well that it is proverbial with all politicians in the county of York.
The Budget-Mr. Veniot

Now let me say that upon the return of the deputy minister I was notified that certain changes had been made in the regulations against which I had protested on the floor of this house, but what did the hon. member for Northumberland accomplish? He accompanied the deputy minister, though whether he went beyond his own county I do not know. The deputy minister held meetings in Restigouche county, where the people of Gloucester, whom I have the honour to represent, went to meet him. He also had a meeting in Chatham and another in St. John. When the deputy minister came back he recommended new regulations, and what do we find? While most of the vicious regulations were cancelled and the old regulations put back in force, we find as I showed the house later on, that one of the changes wa^ worse than the regulation complained of; in other words, the remedy was worse than the disease. My hon. friend from Northumberland, if he is to claim credit for having accomplished this change, has my pity when he undertakes to explain to the people of the county which he represents this fisheries regulation to which I now refer.
Now, Mr. Speaker, having finished paying my compliments to the hon. member for Northumberland I wish to pay my compliments to the Minister of Fisheries before proceeding to discuss the budget. In order to be quite correct in what I am about to say I am going to quote from the speech of my hon. friend the minister as it appears in Hansard. He was referring to the tariff of 40 cents per ton on anthracite coal, and in his anxiety to placate the users of anthracite coal in Quebec and Ontario he made the following astounding statement:
I submit that that tax, which was held up as a burden placed upon the people of Ontario and Quebec, need not bg paid at all by the people of those provinces. In the first place, even if they buy anthracite coal, the treasury gets the benefit of the tax. It remains to be seen, however, how much of that tax will be paid by the producer. I venture to say, owing to the highly competitive nature of the business. that the larger portion, if not the -whole of that tax. will be paid by the producer in the United States.
I do not hear any applause from the other side of the house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that not correct?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is just what I wanted; I set the trap and I caught my hon. friends. If the American producers are to absorb the duty on anthracite coal, where is the protection for the producers in Nova Scotia? Will my hon. friends answer that? Where is the protection for the coal miners in the
fMr. Veniot.]
province of Nova Scotia? On the other hand what do we find? We have the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) standing up almost immediately after the Minister of Fisheries concluded and saying to this house-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You can depend upon what he said.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
His statement now is not consistent with his statement last year on the floor of this house. Last year he claimed that there should be a duty of at least SI .50 per ton on coal imported into Canada; he insisted upon that in season and out of season, whenever he spoke in this house. He blamed the Liberals because they would not put on a duty of SI AO against coal imported into Canada, yet now he comes to this house and says he is not quite satisfied with the budget in relation to coal, and warns the people that a larger increase must be given later on. I wonder why the hon. gentleman is willing to accept a slight increase to-day when, in the time of Liberal rule, he was demanding $1.50 per ton and saying that if this protection were not given the whole industry in Nova Scotia would be ruined. That is the inconsistency on the part of the hon. gentleman to which I wish to refer. He said further, "I want to warn the people of Ontario and Quebec that we are not satisfied with that 40 cents per ton on anthracite coal." Let my hon. friend take the minister from his province aside and whisper into his ear; let my hon. friend consult with the minister from his province and then perhaps we will be in a position to choose between the two. Who is right, the hon. member for Pictou, who says the duty must be $1.50 per ton, or the Minister of Fisheries, who says the 40 cents per ton will be absorbed by the American producers and therefore will be of no protective benefit to the miners of the province of Nova Scotia? That is the sort of thing we hear from hon. gentlemen opposite. They cried aloud for high protection on coal when the Liberals were in power, but to-day when their own party is in power they are satisfied with a small minimum increase in protection. It all depends, Mr. Speaker, upon whose ox is gored.
One of the other things to which I should like to direct the attention of the house is the statement, made by the Prime Minister during the session last September, that the additional duty then imposed would not mean an increase in price to the consumer. I hold in my hand evidence that that statement is not founded on fact. If the Prime Minister was given such a guarantee, then those who gave it did not carry out their engagement.

The Budget-Mr. Veniot
In order to prove what I say, I will give an illustration. I hold in my hand an invoice from a firm manufacturing rubber stamps and other rubber goods in the city of Toronto, Charles W. Mack. Written across the face of this invoice, in fact printed across the face, are these words:
Increase in price due to change in tariff.
Does anyone need further positive evidence?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They only make rubber stamps and nothing else.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what you should have placed over you. I am sorry the onion member, or rather I should say the representative of onions in the province of Ontario, is not in the house. This would be interesting to him.

speechtext:
Since my hon. friend has guessed at it we will leave it at that, though he is far astray. I have here a circular from the Ontario Onion Growers' Cooperative, dated October 10, 1930, addressed to the trade. This is onion bulletin No. 5, in which they say:
In the belief that Ontario was 'possibly affected more by the present industrial depression than the other provinces, we voluntarily reduced our prices on October 2nd, from 10 cents to 25 cents per bag.
Any applause?
I say voluntarily because, on October 1st, the^ anti-dumping act became effective on onions, giving us a protection against imported onions greater than our f.o.b. quotation. Internally we have no competition.
No wonder.
British Columbia market is firm at a higher f.o.b. price than ours, and it looks as if we have to supply part of the prairie market. Enough said.
Then the circular proceeds:
Don't complain a couple of weeks from now that you couldn't see any possibility of higher prices for onions.
Let me inform the house that onions increased in price from that date. They predicted it; their prediction was borne out, because in November, 1930, onions were selling at $2 per 100 pounds, while in May, 1931, they were selling at $2.36 per 100 pounds.
Let me now deal with the matter of corsets, a subject which is interesting to the ladies of whom I see a number in the gallery. This circular which I hold in my hand reads
In view of the recent upward revisions of the tariff announced by the dominion government, we think that it is only right and proper
that we should remind you that our prices are "subject to change without notice," and as these revisions will undoubtedly increase the manufacturing costs of many lines, it is highly probable that advanced prices may have to be announced in the near future.
This letter is not written with the intention of crying "wolf, wolf," but we feel that it is only fair that our customers should know just what has been happening. Practically all lines of textiles and other supplies used in the manufacture of corsets have been affected by the increases in duty just announced, and this must in time be reflected in increased prices of manufactured goods.
This is from the Woolnough Corsetiers of Toronto.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who prepared that statement for the hon. member?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Nobody prepared it for me. This is the original circular signed by the firm itself, per F. M. Kay. And I want to say to the hon. gentleman that if he would take as great care in the preparation of his speech as I do in regard to mine, he would get along better.
I wish now to call the attention of the Prime Minister, who is also acting as Minister of Finance, to what I consider an injustice to the fishermen of the maritime provinces in connection with the changes in the tariff. Some years ago, in order to encourage the putting up of kippered herring in the maritime provinces, the then government imposed a specific duty in addition to the ad valorem duty on this commodity. If the present government believe it is necessary to have protection to encourage our industries, how is it that they have removed the specific duty on kippered herring put up in the maritime provinces? After the additional protection was afforded some three or four years ago, large sums of money were expended in preparation for putting up this foodstuff, but to-day that specific duty is removed and foreign countries are permitted to offer keen competition in the market that we have for kippered herring.
The Prime Minister, in his budget speech, referred to a large number, eighty-seven in all, of new industries established in the Dominion of Canada. Among that number he mentioned two in the province of New Brunswick. One of those to which he referred is established in the city of St. John, A. W. Higgins Company, a United States company manufacturing fertilizers. This company does not manufacture fertilizers; it imports the ingredients and mixes them. This company was established in 1928 in the city of St. John, and although established in that year in competition with the cooperative farmers who import the ingredients and mix them themselves, it employs only three or four men
The Budget-Mr. Veniot

during the summer time, and about fifteen or twenty during the winter season. According to the Prime Minister the other company is the Summers Fertilizer Company, Incorporated, which is established at St. Stephen, New Brunswick. At the present moment they are employing only four men. In the winter time they employ fifteen or twenty. They do not manufacture; they merely mix fertilizers. These are some of the great factories that have been established.

speechtext: I suppose the hon. gentleman knows that his government closed up a plant at St. Stephen?

speakeroldname: Mr. W. W. KENNEDY (Winnipeg South Centre):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To traverse the budget debate at this late stage in my opinion can avail but little, and it is not my intention to do it. I tjhink this is clear to us all, that the subamendment as proposed by the independent group in this house will receive their unanimous support. It is equally true that the amendment as proposed by the official opposition will be supported by them; we can also assume that the main motion introduced by the government will receive the support of government supporters in this house, and that it will be adopted. That being so, I wish to pass on to three matters which to my mind are of special interest.
The first is a matter of immediate and acute concern. I refer to a matter which already on many occasions has been the subject of discussion in the house, namely, unemployment as existing in Canada to-day and the measures

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
or means by which some remedy may be furnished. I represent, sir, in this house the riding of Winnipeg South Centre, a constituency which is in the heart of that great western city, the third city of Canada, a city in which the problem of unemployment is at present, a matter of immediate and outstanding concern. I wish to approach this question not in any disputatious way, because I think no good can be served by that. I should like first to clear the ground a little.
First I say this question of unemployment is a matter of national concern. That will not be disputed. It is a matter that the people of Canada expect this government to deal with. It is a matter that the people of Canada have a right to expect this government to deal with, and I believe that this government will not disappoint the people of Canada in that regard.
Much has been said, and many words have been bandied across this floor as to just what the present administration during the last campaign promised to do. Many statements have been made, some correct, some partly correct, some greatly exaggerated and unfair. But this stands out. Just about one year ago the Conservative party recognized that the question of unemployment was then one of national concern. It recognizes that it is still a matter of national concern, and it was to the Conservative party on July 28th last that the people of Canada, rightly or wrongly, turned in this their hour of need. The party then, and the government now, has a trust to the Canadian people which I think they will recognize.
What is the situation? I am not going to go into statistics. Many are available, some correct, some incorrect, but this fact remains, that there is unemployment in this country to-day to an extent which calls for the attention of all governments, federal, provincial and municipal. As to whether unemployment is greater in the west now than it was a year ago I am not prepared to say. In some parts of the country certainly it has diminished; in other parts undoubtedly it is greater.
Who are these unemployed? You have witnessed, sir, as I did on May day last, parades of the unemployed. Who are they? I grant that among them there are some professional agitators and demagogues who serve no useful purpose to themselves or to this country. But, sir, there were also extremists watching them from the tall buildings as they paraded by. The number of those two classes of extremists, thank God, is relatively small. The rank and file, the great majority of those people are honest, decent Canadians, seeking what? Not coins in their hats, but
work. To afford those people that chance should be Canada's chief concern. Who will shoulder the burden? I shall not enter into any argument as to where the line should be drawn as between the federal, provincial and municipal authorities respecting jurisdiction in the matter of unemployment relief. Surely it is a job for them all. The principle has been recognized by both parties that once unemployment has reached the stage that it becomes a matter of national concern, there is imposed upon the federal government the duty of stepping in; and that is right. Take any centre you like. Take the city of Winnipeg, with the unemployed there last winter, as they are now, and as they will be, it is apprehended, this fall, and call the roll. Not by any means all citizens of Winnipeg, in the real sense of the word, but residents of Canada, who, in the very nature of things, drift into a large city where they think there is the greatest hope of relief. Already many of the municipalities which have been least able financially to stand the burden have reached their limit. The city of Winnipeg, I am informed,-I should like to be corrected if I am wrong-expended of its own money in the past year, for this purpose, nearly three-quarters of a million dollars. It behooves us then to consider the matter thoroughly and arrive at some basis upon which the difficulties which we will meet during the coming winter may be taken care of. The criticism may be offered, and in fact has been frequently made, that to declare such difficulties is not good advertising for any part of the country. But surely the way to solve a problem is first to face the facts. I do not wish to be quoted as indicating that I am unduly apprehensive or that the people of Winnipeg have become panicky, because that is not the fact. They have carried through this period of depression and they will continue to do so. I wish however to draw the attention of the house to the fact that people in centres such as Winnipeg and Vancouver expect that this matter will be dealt with. And I have no doubt whatever that it will be dealt with; I have every assurance in that respect.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what has been done? The right hon. leader of the opposition, at the conclusion of the marathon speech he delivered yesterday, referring to unemployment, made the following statement:
The ministry have done nothing to meet the present situation.
When a member who has sat as long in the
house as my right hon. friend, particularly one who occupies a position as import-

Then follow the figures. The right hon. leader of the opposition derides this relief and says nothing has been done. I ask hon. members to compare what the present government has actually done with what the right hon. leader of the opposition was willing to do less than one year ago. What he was willing to do needs no repetition by me; his actions are known to this house and to the electors of Canada. Yesterday the right hon. gentleman asked: "Where is Senator Robertson, the Minister of Labour? Why is he not here?'' Let me suggest that the Minister of Labour in going through the western country, visiting the principal centres of employment, interviewing chief civic officials, getting in touch with labour and municipal organizations, carrying out a survey such as that throughout Canada, is rendering a service immeasurably more valuable than if he had listened to the four-hour speech of my right hon. friend. I make this statement without any disrespect whatever for the right hon. gentleman.
The right hon. leader of the opposition has referred to conferences. This house and the people of Canada expect deeds, not mere words. If there is any outstanding characteristic of the present government it is that it acts rather than talks. What is to be gained by such criticism as that lodged yesterday by the leader of the opposition? As a new member I found myself wondering why, after so many years of parliamentary experience, an hon. member would spend four hours flailing threshed straw. What purpose could be served? I may be wrong, but the thought occurred to me that the right hon. leader of

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
the opposition is so completely obsessed with the idea that he was born to rule that he is unhappy every minute he finds himself sitting on the opposite side of the house. For over three hours the right hon. gentleman criticized. I do not wish to be disrespectful, but for the want of a word which may be somewhat more parliamentary I would describe his criticism as three hours of "pooh-bah." He seems to forget that most of the matters with which he was dealing are of the past. This is the present; to-morrow is dawning; it is tomorrow with which we should be dealing.
In closing my discussion of unemployment, I make the following suggestions, Mr. Speaker. First, I suggest that there be made a complete survey-this I believe is being done already and has proceeded a considerable way-of the actual conditions as to unemployment existing in this country to-day and, as is apprehended, will exist when the winter approaches. Knowing those conditions, then adequate steps can be taken to deal with them. The right hon. leader of the opposition suggested a conference-not an unreasonable suggestion. Certainly conferences are being held now by the Minister of Labour with those who are in direct contact with unemployment conditions in various parts of the country. If in addition to that it be essential, as it probably will be, to meet with the provinces to work out the basis of a solution, then it is fitting that such a conference should be held in ample time to take action before the winter season is on us. What will be done is not for me to say, as I do not know; but it does seem to me that something should be done along the lines on which the government has already proceeded, namely, the initiation of a vigorous policy of construction of public works, such as highways, public buildings, and other federal undertakings at present needed. And it is not too much to expect that to create employment we shall have to anticipate to some extent the needs of the future. For that purpose it is obvious that revenues will not meet such a program, and I suggest that a federal loan be floated. I have no doubt that the people of Canada would subscribe enthusiastically to such a loan. The moneys thus raised could be expended not by way of doles, but in the construction of needed public works. This would not be wasteful expenditure, but a wise investment. It would enable us to tide over this period of unemployment until better times come, and we all hope that they are fast approaching. Such a proposal, Mr. Speaker, is not unfair. We of to-day are
carrying the burdens of yesterday. Is it too much to ask that the generation of to-morrow lend a helping hand?

May I make one personal reference? I understand that my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) is to follow me. During the July campaign in the city of Winnipeg there was displayed on one of the windows of my committee room this slogan: "Kill the spectre of unemployment!" Now, my opponent spent a good deal of time talking about that slogan. I understand that my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) also took a crack at it, speaking over the radio at Brandon. I did not mind that a)t all, but the argument pursued by them was that unemployment is a world wide condition; so how could any party in Canada hope to cure it- how could Canada do anything to kill the spectre of unemployment? By way of reply just let me use one illustration. Our concern is " Canada first." I know it is very fine to look upon the world as a brotherhood and to say that we must not raise the tariff here because if it builds up Canadian industry it will throw brother workmen out of employment in Japan, Russia or somewhere else. But I am not unselfish to that extent. I conceive it my duty as representing a Canadian constituency to work for Canada first, to build up industry here; if it gives employment to Canadian workmen at the expense of workmen in Japan or Russia or elsewhere, still my duty is to Canada. Now if the policy which this government is pursuing as to building up industry in this country, as to working up our raw material in Canadian factories by Canadian workmen, creates additional employment, as we have ample evidence it does, then I say this: Every head of a Canadian family who is out of employment and in destitution, is downhearted and depressed and hopeless, when he gets a job in one of these factories and at the end of the first week comes home with his pay envelope, as he gathers around the table that night with his little family of six or seven, assured of steady work-I say that in each such case you drive out of the eyes of that family the look of depression and despair, and place there instead the light of hope. In a word, for them you banish the spectre of unemployment, that is something worth while. Multiply that case a hundredfold or a thousandfold, and surely it is something worth trying to do, surely it is
