However, I am not going into that to-night. I was very glad the last speaker recognized the seriousness of the unemployment situation. He suggested that there should be a careful survey, and also that conferences should be held in ample time. I wonder whether he saw the despatch from Victoria which came
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

to us two days ago, stating that Senator Robertson had declared that a dominion-provincial summer conference was not advisable. That seems bo me a most deplorable statement. Those of us who come from the west at least, who for the last year have been feeling the full pressure of unemployment, had hoped that there would be a conference between the dominion and the provinces in order that arrangements could be made in the very near future. I am greatly disappointed that there should have come an announcement of this kind, and I hope the government will reconsider the decision. Only a few days ago since another despatch brought word to us that troops actually had been sent to Edmonton in order to be on hand in case of riots which were threatened. speechtext:
That may be tTue, but the fact is that although we give the present administration full credit for having called a special session of parliament; although we gave them that credit at the time and have done so since, still we have serious unemployment. In view of the acute situation it seems to me that immediate action ought to be taken. I do not want to refer to the past too much, but after all the government is the responsible body. Just a year ago the Prime Minister, speaking in Calgary, was reported in the Calgary Herald of June 13 as having said:
This is a new country and there is no excuse for unemployment in Canada if a government does its duty.
That is all I want to say; there is no excuse for unemployment in Canada if a government does its duty. The Prime Minister went on:
I am convinced this unemployment has now ceased to be local and provincial and has
[Mr. Woodsworth.1
become national in its importance. It has reached far beyond the narrow confines of Calgary or Alberta and is stretching into the broad confines of our dominion.
I think the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre will quite agree with that statement, as I myself agree with it, but I find that the Acting Minister of Labour attempts to get out of the responsibility for existing unemployment by saying it is primarily a municipal matter. Again, speaking at Woodstock on June 26 of last year, the present Prime Minister, as reported by the Toronto Mail and Empire, said:
We must pass laws at the special session that will anticipate work for our people on national highways, on great canals that we must make for our waterways to the sea, in great undertakings such as branch lines and matters of that kind in order that we may give employment to our people.
All I want is action. But, Mr. Speaker, there is one thing to which I must refer tonight, and that is the demoralizing effect upon the unemployed of these long periods when they have to subsist largely through charity. Only a few days ago I had a letter from a friend of mine, a lady now resident in Ontario, who wrote with regard to an immigrant boy. I will read a paragraph, since though this refers to a special case it is typical of a great many cases:
Late last fall a neighbour of my sister's picked up a boy who had no work nor any money, so he took him home, paid him for some farm work and then, winter setting in, told him he could keep him for the winter but with no pay. This was to be his second winter of farm labour with no pay. During the winter he came to my sister's house-as she had an immigrant boy-together they built birdhouses in the evening and the family here played games with them. My sister says a nicer boy would have been hard to find. In February he left with another immigrant boy to find work. Nothing more was heard from the lad until about a month ago-ha came back. In the meantime he has travelled on the freight trains back and forth twice to Halifax hoping to get back home.
That is to the old country.
During this time he has been sleeping in jails, eating in soup kitchens and been chased from town to town by the police. It would not be hard to know the result of all this- he is here with my sister. She has taken him on for a month, but feels she can't do more than this. But what of the boy as a result of his two years in Canada? He has lost his selfrespect, changed from a dapper lad to a tramp in appearance. He has lost his respect for everything sacred, entirely embittered and discouraged, the makings I would say of a criminal if allowed to drift back into the tramp life again.
She makes a plea that he might be deported, and that if possible more boys

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
be prevented from emigrating to this country. I would call upon the members of this house, who are not without human sympathy, to think over the serious demoralization which is taking place in the cases of so many thousands of our people, which inevitably will drive them into crime.
The amendment to the amendment, in urging immediate action, refers to the crisis in 1914. At that time the government of Canada passed a law that bank notes no longer should need to be redeemed in gold. They took that action at that time in the interests of the banks, lest there should be a run on the banks. The amendment asks that something of this character should be done now in the interests of the people at large. That is the meaning of the anti-deflation proposal. I for one-and possibly I may differ from some other members of this group never have believed that money reform was a cure-all, but I would urge that it would at least temporarily help the producers. Further than that-and this appeals to me-it would relieve the burden of unjust debts.
An economist, a friend of mine, wrote me the other day with regard to this proposal as follows:
A higher internal price level would lower the real burden of all payments of interest, and other contractual payments made in Canadian dollars, whether they were interest on the national debt, on railroad or industrial bonds or stocks, or on bank loans, mortgages, or rents, royalties, or taxes.
It may be objected that while such a change benefits debtors, it is at the expense of creditors.
This is true.
But it simply involves putting creditors back to their position in the years prior to 1929, when the relations of debtors and creditors were considered satisfactory, and permitted an unprecedented prosperity for most producers. There is no reason to believe that the mishap of the recent deflation brings with it any natural justice, any more than the mishap of an epidemic does. A return to the price level of 1922-29 would be a restoration of justice, not a departure from it.

speechtext:
I am not giving
the name. I am giving his statement merely as a summary, not as an authority. The other day, only on June 13, Sir Basil Blackett, who is well known as a director of the Bank of England, apparently, according to a press dispatch, comes to the support of this amendment, because he insists that there must be drastic reorganization of the world's currency system. In his view the way to keep currency sound is to ensure that at all times its volume be neither too great nor too small for the world's needs, but regulated so as to keep prices stable.
Not only is this director of the Bank of England thinking along this line, but I might call attention to a well known monthly letter published by the Royal Bank of Canada. Let me quote a paragraph or so from the June number. This follows a careful study of the volume of production:
This relationship between volume of production and trade and volume of credit is one of the most important discoveries which has ever been made by the statistician. It implies that there is a mathematical relationship between volume of production and credit on the one hand, and the price level on the other. In fact, by dividing each given volume of credit by the corresponding volume of production, the level of prices at any particular moment is approximated.
Again:
The accuracy with which the line showing the theoretical price level corresponds to the actual price level is, in itself, a remarkable verification of the quantity theory of money.
Again:
When volume of credit is increased more rapidly than production, prices rise; when production increases more rapidly than volume of credit, prices fall.
This is his conclusion:
What is the inference to be drawn from the facts which we have outlined? Can it be that had the growth of credit paralleled the increase in volume of production and trade there would have been no substantial changes in the general price level, no major business cycles, no booms, no severe depression? This is indeed a startling concept, affording hope that the social injustices inherent in all major changes in the general price level might be avoided by proper control of credit. This is surely a counsel of perfection not fully attainable in human affairs, but it is clearly within the power of the great central banks, through appropriate interest rates and open market policies, to control within reasonable limits too rapid increase in the volume of credit and also to prevent contraction of the normal growth of credit, which is the basis of the present world tragedy.
It seems to me when eminent authorities are thinking along these lines, it is well that we in
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

this house should give greater attention to the matter, so I have no hesitation in voting for the subamendment which suggests a certain measure of inflation. I like to think of it as anti-deflation. It is but putting us back where we were when most of our debts were contracted. I wonder if I might read a little rhymed prose, as he calls it, which was recently published by Sir Thomas White, originally in the Morning Post. It refers particularly to conditions in the United States, although it is becoming true very rapidly of the class that in Canada to-day controls wealth:
Gold, gold, gold, gold!
Here I sit with wealth untold;
Gold in hand and gold in store,
Vaults and coffers flowing o'er;
Gold in coin and gold in bar,
Gold from near and gold from far,
Gained in peace and gained in war,
Gold, gold, gold, gold.
Here I sit with wealth untold.
They bought our goods, we have their gold, But though I sit with wealth untold,
I am unhappy, for behold-
My people suffer sore distress,
Hunger and want and wretchedness,
And languish in their idleness.
Their hands no longer train the vine,
They cannot sell their corn and wine,
The merchants buy from us no more,
For we have all their golden store,
Their gold, gold, gold, gold!
And here I sit with wealth untold.
There is another stanza, but I shall not read more. That was written by Sir Thomas White simply, as he says, to emphasize the situation in which the United States finds itself to-day and which exists to a very considerable extent for certain classes in Canada who imagine they can continue to pile up dividends at a time when the people cannot buy what has already been produced.
The subamendment goes further than this concrete suggestion, and I am particularly interested in the wider statements of the subamendment. Our amendment goes so far as to advocate a new economic system based on cooperative principles, not on competition, involving the mobilization of our natural resources, technical equipment and financial machinery to provide for the needs of the people. I know this seems heretical to many hon. members. We have been accustomed to deride socialism so that when a socialistic amendment of this kind is put forward, people look askance at it. Yet I would point out that various important bodies are coming very near to the lines of the subamendment. The other night I referred in passing to the pope's encyclical recently published. What does it say? As the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) pointed out the other night, certain 
parts are being emphasized; others are not being stressed so much. The encyclical, as summarized by the Toronto Star of June 12, states:
The present economic life is hard, cruel and relentless in ghastly measure. Two evils arise from modern industrialism: one is an economic abasement of the workman; the other is moral degradation of both employers and employees.
Free competition permits the survival only of those who are strongest, which often means those who fight most relentlessly, who pay the least heed to the dictates of conscience.
There are vast differences between the few who hold excessive wealth and the many who live in destitution. Every effort, therefore, must be made that a just share only of the fruits of production be permitted to accumulate in the hands of the wealthy and that an ample sufficiency be supplied to the workingman.
Unemployment is a dreadful scourge. Social justice demands that reforms be introduced without delay which will guarantee every adult working man a sufficient wage.
That is what we have been asking for in this house for years, and yet that is a condition which seems to be yet far off in the future. Recently there have been held conferences of the United church, which I understand is one of the largest Protestant bodies in this country. The other day the Toronto conference passed this resolution:
That this conference is convinced that the present distressful and obstinately threatening economic situation calls for an even more comprehensive organization of the human and economic resources of the dominion than was imperative in the war.
Almost the very words that we are using in our amendment, pointing out as we do that we have a crisis to-day as severe as that which existed in 1914. The resolution goes on:
We therefore urge that the federal government at the very earliest hour availing itself by commission or otherwise of the ablest and most experienced representatives of agriculture, industry, labour and finance, and of acknowledged experts in economic sciences, should devise a national plan which would direct and organize the total man power and the money power of the dominion, which will find work for the workless, kindle hope in the despondent and bitter, and guide our country into a closer union than we have ever known.
Again, almost the words that are used in our amendment when we urge that there should be a central plan in order that we may more fully and efficiently mobilize the forces of production and distribution in this country.
Perhaps the most radical of all the resolutions passed by the United church was that passed by the Alberta conference. I wish the Prime Minister were present, because I

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
think he is in very close touch with the Alberta conference of the United church. I read a few sentences:
We should proceed as rapidly as possible to the creation of an order based on cooperation and service which would displace the present competitive acquisitive social order.	[DOT]
Again:
Up to the present the central feature of the economic situation is profit.
Again:
The present system has now been under trial for a sufficient period to lend itself to fair criticism and the present unhappy conditions of over-producton, unemployment and attendant uncertainties is its condemnation.
Here we have this church body definitely condemning the present economic system under which we are living. The resolution goes on:
We believe that society should regard forced unemployment as an intolerable menace producing an unemployable class, with slum conditions, wastage of human energy and personality and threatening war or revolution. Governments should grapple with this problem with energy similar to that which would be used in a national emergency.
I have taken the time to read these resolutions in order that the house may become aware that there is a large body of thoughtful opinion outside this house which is very much dissatisfied with the existing economic system and is looking forward to some very radical changes.
Socialism, which is the word most commonly used to describe a new system of which many dream, has often been misunderstood and misinterpreted. May I take a few minutes to show the viewpoint of those who hold this doctrine of socialism which distinguishes some of us alike from the older parties, the Conservatives and the Liberals.
In the earlier days, prior to 150 years ago, each individual workman produced with his own hands a few simple things which he needed for himself, or which he exchanged with others about him. Then came the introduction of power machinery, and on top of that the organization of industry. This process has gone on and on and on until we have to-day the present highly organized system of production and distribution which has spread throughout the world. When the machine came into existence, if the workers themselves could have owned the machine, if the machine itself could have been used in the interests of the community, I think we would have been saved all these difficulties which we now face. But unfortunately the machine became the property of an individual
or of a few individuals; and as these machines have multiplied, as the organization has gone on, we have found that a few individuals or a few great corporations practically control the major part of the productive and distributional machinery that we require today to supply our needs. That development has been accompanied by an entire lack of any social responsibility on the part of those in control. The people who control the machine, and the people who control the organization, the people who control the banks, the railways and the big factories, think that they are justified in running these things in their own interests, without any immediate responsibility to their employees or to the public at large. That, it seems to me, is where the weakness of the present system manifests itself, and some of us would claim that under these circumstances we must so change the system that this great organization will in some way come under collective control, will in some way come under the administration of the people themselves, and will be used not merely to pile up profits for a few but used rather in the interests of the great majority of the people. That is what we call socialism. Socialism, so understood, is not such a very long way from what is adumbrated in the application of the principles enunciated in the pope's encyclical- even though the pope may denounce "socialism." I take it that that is exactly what is meant by those who put forward those resolutions of the United church, even though those who did so may not be followed by the great body of the people of the United church.
One trouble with the present system is that there has been an extension of the idea of private property to cover corporate property. Private property is something that I own for myself, something personal. That was the original idea of the word "proprius"-something of my 'own, a personal thing, but we have extended the meaning until great corporations now claim as their own vast banks and other institutions, and claim them without any responsibility to the public. I submit that this extended idea of property must be challenged, and changed in the interests of those who want to have a tiny bit of property for themselves.
As my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) said this af-ternon, tihe great question which is under discussion in labour circles is this: Will this change in the system be brought in by evolution, by a gradual process, or by a revolution? In Russia it was brought in by
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

revolution following the disasters consequent upon the war. What is going to happen in this country? A good many of us have dreamed that tihese changes could be brought in by gradual steps, but one begins to doubt this. An editor in the west remarked the other day that an explosion does not come gradually. If we allow distress to go on unrelieved, if we allow resentment bo be pent up in the minds of large numbers of people, then sooner or later in this country as in other countries we shall have an explosion. As my hon. friend from Labelle pointed out so clearly the other night, that has been the result throughout history. It is for us to decide by which means we are to bring about the necessary changes.
I have always urged that we use our brains instead of leaving matters until riots force us to take action. I still think there is a possibility of using our brains and yet, as I have watched the action of those in authority this year, not merely the government but those who stand behind the government, the great manufacturing bodies, the banks and the like, those who are really in control, I have wondered whether it is indeed possible that these changes may come gradually. When we propose even a comparatively small change, for instance the lessening of the rate of interest,-to say nothing about sweeping away interest-immediately the whole of the financial fraternity is up in arms. When we propose the lessening of taxes on the necessities of life used by the ordinary people, again we find decided opposition. If as was done at a United church conference the other day, we in this house proposed a moratorium in order that working people would not lose their homes, and that farmers would not be forced to abandon their farms, I know that in this house to-night there would be steady opposition. Indeed hon. members on the government side of the house would be up on their feet in a moment and protest that I was alarming the investors of the country and thus doing irreparable damage. As soon as we make these suggestions involving small changes we meet with opposition. How then can we hope that these gentlemen will consent to the establishment of a new social order?
In the amendment to the amendment there is a suggestion that there should be a scaling down of debts. When I referred to that particular question in my speech on the address in reply I framed my suggestion in that way. My hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) offered the same suggestion in more exact terms when he outlined the measure of inflation. The proposal is that the people who

to-day are holding bonds and mortgages of various kinds should receive interest and final repayment on the basis of the value of the dollar at the time those debts were contracted. To my mind that is not at all unreasonable. Immediately however there is the cry of confiscation. Even the right hon. leader of the opposition, from whom we might have expected some support, told us that to experiment along those lines at a time like this is very, very serious. I suggest that if we cannot secure these minor reforms such as help for the farmer by a reduction of freight rates, even though that reduction involves an additional burden upon the rest of the community-if we cannot secure help for the unemployed, even though we have to tax the rest of the people more heavily in order to keep those unemployed; if we cannot obtain some relief for the debtor class in the form of deflation or scaling down of debts or whatever form such relief may take without immediate protest, 1 say to those in authority that they are simply piling up trouble for themselves in days to come. I do not believe the people in this country are going to stand very much more. I do not think they are going to stand very much more-

Mr. Speaker, in addressing the house for the first time, may I congratulate you on your election to the speakership of the House of Commons, and on the dignity, impartiality and courtesy with which you discharge the duties of your high office. Imbued with the principles which guided the Fathers of Confederation in framing the Canadian constitution, making your own that thought expressed by Sir John A. Macdonald, that there is in this country no conquering race, no vanquished race, but two great races which, in harmony, bonne entente and on an equal footing, must work together in building the Canadian nation, with deference for the two official languages of the country, you had no hesitation in undertaking the arduous task of learning French and expressing yourself in that language in the discharge of the duties incumbent on you as Speaker of this house.
Permit me, sir, to congratulate the hon. member for Toronto Northeast (Mr. Baker) for the courtesy shown towards the French
Canadian race in expressing himself in our Mother tongue. Let me assure him of the gratitude of all my compartiots.
Why is it that at a time when the leading Canadian statesmen are working together to promote feelings of bonne entente between English and French speaking Canadians, why is it, sir, that the Anderson government has launched an unjust attack against the most sacred and cherished rights of French speaking Canadians, against the free teaching of French and religion in the schools of Saskatchewan? I deem it my duty to strongly protest on behalf of myself and constituents against the campaign of national disruption which is carried on in Saskatchewan, against the anti-national legislation put into force by the coalition government of Saskatchewan. The province of Quebec entered into a contract when she associated herself with the other provinces in order to form the Canadian Confederation, and with pride I can loudly proclaim that my province has never made any attempt against the rights of the minorities which she undertook to protect and maintain. Our legislators did not endeavour to seek law texts, and discover in conventions motives to attack the rights of minorities which they had agreed to respect. This question which refers .to the rights of French speaking Canadians should not be discussed on political platforms during an election. I think that public men of all political shades should unite on this most important question and rise above political prejudice in order to foster bonne entente and harmony between the two great races which united to form the Canadian nation.
Allow me, sir, to compliment the distinguished members of the Press Gallery;
I know that they are all proud of their fine profession, that they have the serious duty to enlighten the people on the legislation and questions which are discussed and solved in this house. I trust they will be indulgent for one who speaks for the first time in this chamber rendered so illustrious by many famous debaters.
I deem it a duty and pleasure to again offer my sincere thanks to the people of the beautiful county of Matane for the honour they have bestowed upon me by electing me to this house. They may rest assured that I shall do my utmost to promote the true interests of my county and country.
The county of Matane comprises two constituencies, each having its representative in the Quebec legislature: that of Matane and Matapedia. The provincial constituency of Matane includes the parishes located for

The Budget-Mr. Larue

the most part along or close by the shores of the St. Lawrence river, and its population is made up of farmers, workmen and fishermen.
The improvement of water transportation is a problem which interests in the highest degree the people of my county. The parishes of Metis and Capucins have immediate need of wharfs. The Baie-des-Sables wharf, to be of any use should be extended at least 400 feet. The wharfs of Riviere-Blanche, St-Felecite, de Grosses-Roches and Mechins also need many improvements. The main harbour of the district is that of Matane situated at the opening of the river bearing that name. The completion of the work, begun some years ago, is necessary not only in the interest of the town of Matane but in that of all the neighbouring parishes. At the extreme end of the two breakwater wharfs built on each side of the river, at its opening, sand accumulates during the winter which in the spring partly obstructs the entrance to the harbour.
Each year, dredging must be carried on. This nuisance would entirely disappear if the breakwater wharfs were extended a few hundred feelt. If this work was carried out, boats of an average tonnage, such as those which ply betwen Quebec, the north coast and Newfoundland, could easily enter the harbour of Matane. This would promote, to the great advantage of Matane and the adjacent parishes, a trade intercourse between the south and north shores. The farm products of the county of Matane would benefit by having a market easy of access.
There is another question of vital importance to the Matane district, namely the aid which must be given to the fishermen. We are dealing with excellent people, honest and laborious who need assistance to provide themselves with the necessities of life. Grants must be extended to the fishermen in order to carry out the work of removing dangerous rocks which lie at the bottom of rivers. This would permit small fishing crafts to enter and leave their shelter.
The county of Matane is partly served by the Canada Gulf and Terminal Railway from Mont-Joli to Matane. The freight rates are high and the service is far from being perfect. This railway line shauld be extended to the wharfs of the Matane Harbour so as to cut down the freight cost on goods which are shipped from that harbour. In order to improve the service, in the interest of this district, this railway line should be purchased by the National Railways. Objections might be made that the cost would be prohibitive, however. I think that it is more important for a

state railway system to give a good service to the country than to purchase luxurious hotels abroad.
I now come to the constituency of Matapedia, whose population is made up for the most part of farmers, settlers and workmen. In this constituency which is located in the interior, the main line of communication and transportation is that of the Canadian National Railway.
I may say that the service, on the whole, is not very good in that section. The principal passenger trains running from Montreal to Halifax and vice versa, pass during the night when there are practically no railway agents at the stations. This means that the service is far from being satisfactory, that people cannot obtain railway tickets nor any information as to train arrivals and must at times perform the duties of baggage master. This section is one of predilection for the Canadian National Railway officials when they wish to economize. Two stations are to be soon deprived of their agents. We are wondering if the Canadian National Railway intend soon to have the trains run without their conductors, brakesmen and even without locomotives. No such service would be tolerated in any other district, and I strongly protest against this high handed way of treating the Matapedia valley.
Matapedia county comprises a number of large villages, and public buildings are needed in many localities. For a number of years past there has been question of constructing a railway line which would penetrate to the interior of the Gaspe peninsula. The preliminary survey has been done and plans have been prepared by engineers previous to every election, at the request of the preceding administration. The construction of this railway is necessary to the development of settlements in that section of the country, it would greatly help the parishes which have been opened to settlers and would serve at least .thirty parishes in the Gaspe peninsula.
Mr. Esdras Minville, a Montreal professor, published last autumn, in the newspaper "Le Devoir" very extensive, interesting and instructive articles on this subject. I am aware that, in the present circumstances, with a deficit inherited from the former administration, it is difficult for this government to grant all the requests we make; however, under the able leadership of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, I feel confident that before long the country will find an era of prosperity which can rightly be expected with the leader that presides over its destinies, and then the people of the county of Matane-comprising the

The Budget-Mr. Seguin
constituencies of Matane and Matapedia-will have the service to which it is entitled. I earnestly request the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) not to ignore my county like his predecessors on the other side of the house did, I beg of him to remember that the county of Matane is located in Canada and thereby is entitled to its fair quota of the public funds voted by the house for public utilities.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I deem it my duty to
express on behalf of the people of l'Assomp-tion-Montcalm, which I have the honour of representing in the house, their appreciation of the budget presented by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), equally Minister of Finance.
I twice carefully read the speech of the right hon. Prime Minister and I endeavoured, by all possible means, to find in what way this budget can relieve unemployment at present prevailing in this country, and especially, how the provisions mentioned in his speech can help that so indispensable part of our population, namely, the farming class;
I was unable to discover anything which can inspire the least hope of relief to either of them. I know that I reecho the feelings of the great majority of the people of Canada and especially those of my section in stating, openly, that the present government being unable to announce, through the mouthpiece of its Prime Minister, any measure in keeping with the numerous pledges made to the people at the last election, deserves to be highly censured for its administration of the affairs of this country. It is no secret that even among the most earnest followers of the government, in the house and throughout the country, there is a large number of them who do not conceal their utter condemnation of the government's policy.
I have not the least doubt, sir, that at present, the right hon. Prime Minister is fully aware that it is much easier to promise the moon than to deliver it.
Where are these great reformers, these great savers of the people who, in 1930, were to bring back prosperity by relieving unemployment and obtaining for the farmers better prices for their products, and more especially for their butter? All will recall the unkept pledges made by the leader of the government and his candidates in the course of the last election. Prosperity was to knock at every door in Canada.
An emergency session was to definitely settle the question of unemployment, and butter, especially, was to command a much 22110-1751
better price the moment they took the matter in hand.
Three months, six months passed, and now the government have been nine months in office and what insignificant results have we witnessed! We can well say that the mountain in labour has brought forth a mouse.
Who has forgotten the alluring and exaggerated appeals made on the political platforms during the election campaign of June and July, 1930?
As the economic crisis, which was spreading throughout the world, had begun to be per-oeptibly felt, it was an easy matter for these gentlemen to frighten the people and gain their sympathies by means of pledges easy to make but hard to fulfil. Is it not a fact, sir, that, at the time, the existing depression was blamed entirely on the government and the King administration was charged of being responsible for this economic crisis.
If the government of that day is to be held responsible-according to the leader of the present administration-is it not a fact that, depression having become more acute, unemployment having increased fivefold, our farmers finding no sale for their products, even at ridiculously low prices, we must conclude that the panacea proclaimed by Mr. Bennett and his followers was but a decoy to the discredit of this government.
And if to-morrow, one year after the July election, the Canadian people were called to again register their vote, there is not the shadow of a doubt that this government would be overwhelmingly defeated; however as it has a five year mandate, the people must be patient and prepare to have their turn while praying Divine Providence to save them from starvation. May I ask, sir, whether that so boasted protective policy which the government have inaugurated brought back prosperity? Has it provided more work, and thereby, brought more comfort in the Canadian homes?
As an outcome of tariff changes carried out at the emergency session, the farmers have to pay dearer for what they purchase, while what they sell does not even give them a fair return for their labour.
I have had sir, the occasion of stating, and I have not the slightest hesitation of repeating it, though I am a Liberal, that I request the utmost protection for all that pertains to agriculture either directly or indirectly. I am in favour of any measure of protection which will result in raising the price of butter, grain, vegetables, in brief all farm products. With reference, especially, to tobacco, it seems that it would be an easy matter for

The Budget-Mr. Seguin
the government to increase the price since it would only need slight changes in the excise taxes and customs duties.
Is it not a fact and a very deplorable one to note that butter-which was used by our opponents as a great battle cry in 1930, when it sold at 34 and 35 cent per pound-retails to-day at 20 and 22 cents; that cheese which sold last year from 15 to 19 cents per pound, sells to-day from 10 to 13 cents; that eggs which sold from 35 to 40 cents per dozen last year, sell to-day 19 to 20 cents? What are we to think of meat which sells at ridiculous prices, prices unheard of for 30 years? Vegetables, among others, potatoes, were practically given away last spring for 15 and 20 cents a bushel, and in a number of cases found no purchaser.
I hear our opponents saying: What is ^ the use of all this recrimination since the crisis is a world-wide one and that the government is not quite responsible for it?
But, sir, if in 1930 the government of the day was held responsible for being the cause of this crisis, according to our opponents who then strongly appealed to the people to cast their votes in their favour in order to wipe out all these ills, are we not justified to-day in telling them that they deliberately deceived the people and after having stolen their mandate they give proof of the worse helplessness?
With reference, sir, to a question which greatly interests a number of people in my district, allow me to refer to the subject of tobacco. I must state, to the credit of the Liberal party, that this industry became a paying proposition when the Liberal government specially took up the matter. In 189i, at the suggestion of the Hon. Mr. Brodeur, then Minister of Inland Revenue, the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier put a duty of 10 cents a pound on imported tobacco; afterwards, and gradually, the Liberal administration increased this duty to 40 and 42 cents. This progressive increase of customs duties levied on imported tobacco developed in Canada and more especially in my county an industry which spread almost everywhere.^
At present, it is found that this protection of 40 cents is insufficient and it would be necessary that the excise tax and customs duty be again increased to insure to the tobacco growers better prices for the fruit of their labours.
An important delegation of my section of the country, thinking they would be welcomed recently addressed themselves to my colleague the hon. member for Berthier (Mr. Barrette) so as to be introduced to the
* TMr. Seguin.]
government. To my great surprise and notwithstanding the zeal which my colleague (Mr. Barrette) must have displayed, neither the Prime Minister nor the Minister of Agriculture, who are more especially interested in the matter, took the trouble of coming to listen to the just claims of the tobacco growers of the district of Joliette. They had to entrust the hon. Postmaster General and the Solicitor General with the task of presenting their claims to the Minister of Finance and the cabinet so as to obtain the protection which, in their opinion, is the only way to insure the tobacco growers the reward to which they are entitled. This delegation of tobacco growers received the assurance of the Postmaster General and Solicitor General that their just claims would certainly be looked after, seeing that they had now to deal with a protectionist government. One of the ministers even stated that they could not understand why there had been so much delay in giving their claims due recognition. Reassured by these new promises made wilth the authority of cabinet ministers, our friends, the tobacco growers returned home satisfied that at last they could expect a reasonable reward for their strenuous labours.
Not finding, sir, in the budget speech any sign that the right hon. Minister of Finance took any notice of the request made by the tobacco growers of my district, I must con-elude-as I would not be so unfair as to think that the hon. Postmaster General and the hon. Solicitor General did not lay the claims of the tobacco growers before the Minister of Finance and the cabinet-I must conclude, I say, that their influence was not of sufficient weight or that the right hon. Prime Minister, too busy in looking after the interests of his friends, the manufacturers and high financiers, entirely forgot to consider the claims of our friends, the tobacco growers.
May I, sir, since it is not too late, insist that the government, in order to increase the revenue of Canada, raise the customs duty by at least 50 cents per pound on foreign tobacco with stems, and at least 75 cents per pound on stripped tobacco, as was requested by the memorandum submitted by the delegation which I mentioned. In order to foster the marketing of tobacco, the government should agree to another suggestion of the tobacco growers of my district, namely reducing the excise tax on cigars selling from $1 to $3 per thousand and on manufactured tobacco from twenty to five cents per pound with an additional tax as follows: (a) Five cents per pound on tobacco selling more than sixty cents and not over

The Budget-Mr. Seguin
ninety cents; (b) ten cents per pound on tobacco selling ninety cents and not over SI.20 per pound; (c) fifteen cents per pound on tobacco selling over $120.
Is it not disgraceful to find that the tobacco grower, at present, receives for his labour only eight to ten cents per pound when the government receives an excise tax of twenty cents for the same product manufactured?
Is it not shameful to find that the poor farmer who labours from 7 a.m. and often from 5 a.m. to 7 or 8 p.m. receives for his labour only eight to ten cents per pound while the treasury pockets twenty cents per pound for this tobacco when manufactured?
It is an urgent matter that the government should assist the tobacco grower, first by having enacted the suggested changes to the excise and customs tariff, secondly by endeavouring to find new markets.
With further reference to tobacco, I wish, sir, to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture who I regret is not in his seat,- however I trust his colleagues will remind him,-to a grant made by his predecessor, the Hon. Mr. Motherwell, to the Co-operative Association of Tobacco Growers of the district of Joliette, a grant that the department did not renew after the change of government. It is a matter of $6,666 which was included in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. I would respectfully urge the Minister of Agriculture to authorize the payment of this grant, on which this Co-operative Association depends and which would be of great help to them. I shall further add and assure the minister that if he will redeem the pledges made by my opponents during the last election, and moreover increase this grant to $10,000, I shall thank him and publicly give him all the credit for this act.
There is another industry, sir, which greatly interests quite a number of the farming class of this country and that is the maple sugar industry.
It would be an easy matter to create a dependable income for the maple sugar and syrup producers, if our protectionist government gave this product the protection which it requires and favoured those who need protection.
The United States government, after having placed a duty of 8 cents per pound on our maple sugar, was compelled to reduce this duty to 4 cents, to meet the wishes of the American people who want our maple sugar and syrup; this duty however is still prohibitive, and I think that in order to promote the sugar and syrup industry in this country it behooves the government to grant a rebate
of 5 cents per pound on maple sugar or 50 cents a gallon on maple syrup, when exported.
This would promote the exportation of this product abroad; once it was known it would highly be appreciated and better prices could be obtained, owing to the great demand which would result.
May I, sir, draw the attention of the government to the Bankruptcy Act. I wish to state that this act, so far as it concerns the Canadian fanner and more particularly the farmer of the province of Quebec, is a grievance which should be righted immediately. This act, which is a necessity for trades people, is at present the main cause of the loss of credit suffered by the farming class.
Our farmers find it impossible now to borrow on the security of their farms, because the lender has had to suffer such losses owing to the enforcement of the Bankruptcy Act which permits an unscrupulous assignee to pile up the cost of the liquidation; this often makes the lender lose part of his loan on a first mortgage, notwithstanding the fact that the lender took precautions not to make a loan greater than half of the value of the property mortgaged.
This question is of the utmost importance and I particularly draw the attention of the government to it, requesting them to look into the matter and take the necessary steps to prevent, before it is too late, this Act causing greater havoc in our rural sections.
I also wish, sir, to take the opportunity of inquiring what attitude the government intends to take in connection with the aggressive measures resorted to by the Anderson government against the Roman Catholics and French Canadians of Saskatchewan.
Already, certain ministers of the crown, as well as members on the other side, such as the hon. member for Matane (Mr. Larue) have expressed their views on this question and stated that they greatly sympathized with the minority, which is being deprived of education in the French language, and to which very little religious teaching is given in schools.
It is all very fine, sir, to express sympathy, as did the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre), the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) and the hon. member for Matane (Mr. Larue). This, however, does not alter the situation; what I wish to know is what measures the government intends taking to give justice to the French Canadians and Catholics of the province of Saskatchewan.
All, in the house, know how generously the English and Protestant minority are dealt with in Quebec. Strong evidence of this ha*
275S
The Budget-Mr. Seguin

often been given by our English speaking fellow-citizens from Quebec and by men from other parts who do not speak the language or practise the religion of the great majority of the people of Quebec.
Why, sir, should our people who are so broadminded in Quebec, see their compatriots ostracized and suffer injustice under the rule of a Tory government in Saskatchewan?
What would be the verdict, if the Quebec government, applying the same measure of justice, or rather injustice, inflicted on the English speaking people and on those who are not Roman Catholics in our province, the same treatment which is meted out to the Roman Catholics and French Canadians of Saskatchewan. What an outcry would be raised here in the house and in both the Catholic and Protestant press throughout the country. Yet, this treatment is meted out to the French speaking and Catholic minority of Saskatchewan. Here and there a weak voice, on the government side, is heard protesting; however, the leader himself and the government have not yet expressed their views in this respect; it is, however, high time that this house and the country should know what sentiments they harbour on the subject.
Confederation placed us on an equal footing, as Sir John A. Macdonald stated, and it is high time that we should know whether we were deceived and too credulous.
Before resuming my seat, I wish to glance once more over the budget presented by the right hon. Prime Minister, as Minister of Finance, and again strongly protest against the lack of provision which the budget shows in order to relieve the farmers and the working classes of this country.
Where is the immediate prosperity promised to us at the last election? What has been done and what relief is being afforded to the innumerable army of the unemployed to whom work should be given.
The government instead of fulfilling its pledges to the people, seem to take delight in burdening them by levying new taxes, especially on the middle class and on the one which has the least resources.
Is it not an injustice for instance, to exact a tax of two cents on a cheque of $1, and the same tax on a cheque of $100 or $1,000 or even $100,000? It is evident that the person who has to issue the most cheques for small amounts is the one who has but a small balance to his credit in the bank, and, consequently he should be spared the most. I could apply the same argument to the increase in postage rates and also to the sales tax; however, my time is too limited.
[Mr. Seguin.1
Could not the government have found means to tax the high financial interests, the
large corporations and wealthy companies instead of taking from the pockets of the less fortunate people, what is needed to make up the deficit due to its carelessness?
Mr. Speaker, I shall close my remarks by asking the government to accept my remarks in the spirit in which they are offered and to realize that they were made in the best interests of the farming class, which is without gainsay, the one which is most deserving of the greatest protection on the part of our government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I have but a few minutes at my disposal, I shall confine myself to one matter, namely, the chief argument that has been advanced in this house by hon. gentlemen opposite, that the budget which we are now considering is a rich man's budget. In this regard I should like to refer particularly to the remarks of the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix), who really started the ball rolling. The hon. member for Beauce stated, according to the translation of his speech as it appears on page 2321 of Hansard of June 4:
It is the budget of a man who personally must be immensely wealthy and seeks thereby to protect only the privileged class-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Wait before you applaud. -namely, those who are rich, forgetting entirely that the majority of the people of this country, not to say 99 per cent, is made up of workers who can barely provide for their families.
Later on, the hon. gentleman added these words:
There is also a group of about 25 citizens who are taxed on a revenue of $1,000,000 or more, yearly. The latter have been specially favoured, as my statement will show.
I wish to observe the rules of this house, Mr. Speaker, but I confess I am at a loss to find appropriate words to qualify such a statement. If the hon. gentleman had suggested that there were only 24, or 20, or even 15 persons with such an income, I might qualify his statement as incorrect. But it has been proved, and the hon. gentleman knows it as well as the rest of us, that there is no single person in this dominion with such an income.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who has proved it?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) has proved it-

The man with such an income might have avoided the tax.

The Budget-Mr. Gobeil

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The tax has not been avoided. The fact is that there is not, and there has not been in the last five or ten years a single citizen of Canada with such an income

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who told you?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Who told me? I got the information where any other hon. gentleman can get it. If my hon. friends will go to the proper source they will get the information. This statement is false, and the hon. gentleman knows it. The hon. gentleman also stated that the poor were paying more taxes than under the Liberal regime. Is it not a fact that 26,000 of those who were paying income tax under the former administration will now be exempt? Is it not true that 25,000 persons, who paid income tax on the basis of an exemption of $3,000 will now be relieved of taxation, with the additional exemption of $500? None of them will pay a tax. They are not the rich, and they are not the poorest class in the country; there are hundreds of thousands of people who do not pay income tax, but these are the poorest of those who pay income taxes. There is also another class of people in connection with whom the tax has been reduced; those are the people paying on an income of from $3,500 to $6,000. Those people also have seen their taxes reduced by this budget. They are also among the poorer classes of those who pay income tax.
Let us go a step further and see what was the position when the Liberal government took office in 1921. At this point let me remind the house that until this session Canadians never heard from this party the argument that the Liberals were bringing in a rich man's budget. When the Conservatives went out of office in 1921 the rate of income tax applicable to persons other than corporations were as follows: there was a normal tax of four per cent on incomes up to $6,000 and of eight per cent on incomes in excess of $6,000. There was a supertax of one per cent on incomes over $5,000, increasing to 64 per cent on incomes of $1,000,000. In addition there was a five per cent tax computed on the sum of the normal tax and the supertax. This meant a tax of $696,349.50 on an income of $1,000,000. What did the Liberals do when they came into power? By chapter 10, sections 16 and 17, George V, the King administration repealed the old rates, abolished the normal, the supertax and the five per cent additional tax, and introduced the graduated scale which began at two per cent and increased to 50 per cent on incomes in excess of $500,000. Those rates were reduced further in 1927 by chapter 31, section 17, George V, under which an additional 10 per cent discount was given, leaving the highest rate 45 per cent. Did anyone hear the Conservatives at that time say this was a rich man's budget?
Mr. ST-PERE: They were taxing the new rich.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not catch the remark; if I understood it I think I could reply. A further cut was made in 1928 by chapter 12, sections 18 and 19, George V, the discount being increased from 10 per cent to 20 per cent, which reduced the maximum rate to 40 per cent. After these three decreases the tax on an income of $1,000,000 was reduced from $696,349.50 to $362,928, a difference of 8333,421.50.
On an income of $500,000 the tax under the Conservative government was $318,349.50. This was reduced by the first change under the Liberal government to $203,690. The next reduction made it $183,321, and the last reduction brought the tax on an income of $500,000 to $162,952, or a total reduction of $155,397.50. I want to point out again that in all those years not one member of the Conservative party, then in opposition, accused the Liberal administration of being the party of the rich men or the multi-millionnaires. I am not surprised at that, because it is not the practice of the Conservative party to raise cries of prejudice as between one class and another.
Now I should like to say a few words, if I have time, with regard to the bonus on wheat.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about butter?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We will talk about butter also. Again hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to prejudice one part of the country against another. I say, Mr. Speaker, that if this confederation is to continue and to be a success; if this Canada of ours is to become a great country, every section of this dominion must be prepared to give and take. I am free to admit that hon. members from the west and bon. members from the east lose no opportunity to further the cause of their particular districts, and 1 might add that at times I believe they are not altogether quite fair. As I have said before, however, if we are to have a great country we must be prepared to give and take. There are different forms of bonuses. It is quite true that the provinces of Quebec and Ontario will share the cost of that bonus to the west, but is it not true also that the central part of Canada derives some benefit from the policies pursued by the different governments of Canada?
We had a good illustration of this fact a couple of days ago in the agriculture com-
The Budget-Mr. Gobeil

mittee. Every hon. member knows that this year the price of eggs has been very low, and the farmers of Ontario and Quebec are getting only from 15 to 20 cents per dozen for their eggs. Hon. members representing western constituencies proved to the satisfaction of the committee that, because of transportation costs and other factors, the farmers in the western provinces were getting only from five to eight cents per dozen. Under the constructive policy of this government we have had established in this country over eighty new industries since we came into power, and of that number over seventy-five were established in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Therefore if the people of the west have to pay even a little more for the goods which they are buying from the east- and while I do not think they are paying very much more, I do not deny that in some instances they might pay a little more-I think the majority are paying it quite willingly.
Is it not true that we in the eastern provinces have the benefit of a local market at our doors? While the western farmers are getting eight cents a dozen for their eggs, we are getting twenty cents. Is it not true, as the hon. member for Long Lake (Mr. Cowan) said the other night, that we in the eastern provinces are dependent every year on the millions of dollars that constitute the outcome of the western crop? Let us just take the Marine department. Is it not true that the eastern provinces are every year receiving millions of dollars of which the western provinces must pay their Share? Some hon. members might say that these millions are going for the good of the west as well as of the east. That is true to a certain extent, but at the same time it is also true that every year the citizens of the eastern provinces are benefiting by those millions of dollars that are spent here, our labourers are receiving wages and our farmers are having a local market for their products. When I use the word "citizen," I mean it to include all classes, not excepting the farmers. That is where I claim hon. gentlemen opposite are quite mistaken. The way they talk, it seems to me they regard the farmers of Quebec and Ontario as men almost ready for an asylum. But far from that, the farmers of Quebec and Ontario are intelligent people, and they realize what they are receiving from this government. The other night the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix) and some other members from Quebec said that members on this side from the province of Quebec would not like to have to go back and face our 
electors. Let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite that any time they want to come to Compton and face the electors there, I am willing they should come.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My offer is to go anywhere and at any time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What we said during the
election campaign was that if the Conservatives came into power, they would see to it, that the farmers of Quebec and Ontario would get the market of the Canadian people for their products. Although it is quite true that the price of butter and cheese is lower than it was last year, I would not be afraid to return to Compton county. I know the farmers of Quebec are satisfied to get their own market for themselves.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I take it for granted that
I am speaking to intelligent people, and when I say the farmers of Quebec are satisfied, it does not mean they would be as well satisfied to get twenty cents as thirty cents a pound for their butter. But we have fulfilled our pledges, and the farmers of Quebec, when they have their own market to themselves, are satisfied to compete with the rest of the world in the butter and cheese industry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us make a bargain: I will resign my seat and you resign yours.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend need not
be so ready to resign his seat. There is no necessity for his resigning his seat or for my resigning mine, but I invite the hon. gentleman to come to Compton county at any time he cares, and I shall meet him on the platform. I can understand why the hon. gentleman would not like to go there. If he were resigning his seat and I mine, I know what we would see in the province of Quebec: we would see what we have seen in the past, campaigns into which race cries and prejudice enter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not in my county. Resign your seat and you will be defeated.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The time for such campaigns is gone and from now on, when the Liberals of Quebec come before the electorate, they will have to talk politics, something which they have not done in the past.
On motion of Mr. McIntosh the debate was
adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
